questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman is being typed before an elective surgery. In the blood-typing kit, antibodies to A, B, and D antigens are fixed to separate membranes and a sample of her red blood cells is added. Agglutination occurs in the anti-B and anti-D wells but not in the anti-A well. Which of the following is her blood type?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A positive

choices.label: B
choices.text: AB positive

choices.label: C
choices.text: B negative

choices.label: D
choices.text: B positive

choices.label: E
choices.text: O negative

explanation.summary: In a blood-typing agglutination kit, clumping indicates that the corresponding antigen is present on the patient's red blood cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Agglutination occurs when antibodies fixed to the membrane bind an antigen present on the red cells and form immune complexes that clump. Clumping with anti-B means the B antigen is present, and clumping with anti-D (Rh) means the cells are Rh positive. No reaction with anti-A means no A antigen. Therefore the blood type is B positive.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A positive would require agglutination in the anti-A well, which did not occur.
whyWrongByChoice.B: AB positive would require agglutination with both anti-A and anti-B; only anti-B reacted.
whyWrongByChoice.C: B negative would show no reaction with anti-D, but anti-D clumping was observed, indicating Rh positive.
whyWrongByChoice.E: O negative cells carry neither A nor B nor D antigen and would not agglutinate in any well.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with type O blood is mistakenly transfused with type A packed red blood cells. Within a few hours he develops fever, hypotension, jaundice, and dark (hemoglobin-containing) urine. Which of the following best explains the underlying mechanism of this reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Failure of neutrophils to mount an oxidative burst against the donor cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation against donor cells (type I hypersensitivity)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Preformed antibodies binding donor red cell surface antigens (type II hypersensitivity)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Soluble antigen-antibody immune complex deposition in vessels (type III hypersensitivity)

choices.label: E
choices.text: T cell-mediated delayed-type response to the donor antigens (type IV hypersensitivity)

explanation.summary: Transfusing incompatible red cells triggers an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction, a type II hypersensitivity reaction.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that a type O recipient has preformed anti-A and anti-B antibodies. When type A red cells are given, these IgM/IgG antibodies bind the cell-surface A antigen and initiate a type II hypersensitivity reaction. The donor red cells are lysed within 24 hours, producing fever, hypotension, hemoglobinuria (blood in the urine), and jaundice.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An oxidative burst defect describes chronic granulomatous disease, unrelated to a transfusion reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Type I hypersensitivity is IgE-mediated allergy, not antibody binding to red cell surface antigens.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type III reactions involve soluble immune complexes deposited in tissues, not antibodies binding fixed cell-surface antigens.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The reaction is rapid and antibody-driven, not a delayed T cell-mediated (type IV) response.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman presents with a malar rash, fatigue, and joint pain. An antinuclear antibody (ANA) test is performed by fixing human cells to a slide, incubating with her serum, and then adding a fluorophore-labeled anti-human IgG antibody. Fluorescence microscopy shows a high-titer homogeneous staining pattern. This pattern is most strongly associated with which of the following conditions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic granulomatous disease

choices.label: B
choices.text: CREST syndrome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Scleroderma

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sjogren syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Systemic lupus erythematosus

explanation.summary: ANA immunofluorescence patterns have known disease associations, and a homogeneous pattern points to SLE.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists specific ANA staining patterns and their associations. The homogeneous pattern is associated with systemic lupus erythematosus. The detection antibody (anti-human IgG) binds the patient's autoantibodies already bound to the fixed cells, and the fluorescence pattern and titer help narrow the differential diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronic granulomatous disease is a neutrophil oxidative burst defect and is not an ANA-defined autoimmune condition.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CREST syndrome is associated with a centromere staining pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Scleroderma is associated with a nucleolar staining pattern, not homogeneous.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sjogren syndrome is associated with a speckled staining pattern.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man has a mildly positive ANA at a low titer but has no symptoms and no evidence of an autoimmune disease on further workup. His physician explains that a low-titer positive ANA can occur without autoimmune disease. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional explanation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A low titer indicates the sample was diluted too little to be interpreted

choices.label: B
choices.text: A positive ANA is diagnostic of lupus regardless of titer

choices.label: C
choices.text: ANA can only be positive in individuals with an active malignancy

choices.label: D
choices.text: ANA titer directly measures the amount of circulating virus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Healthy people can have low-titer ANA

explanation.summary: Titer makes the ANA semi-quantitative, and low-titer positives are common in people without autoimmune disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that healthy people may have positive ANA results at low titers, and that ANA titer can rise in a person without an autoimmune disorder due to some acute infections, chronic infections, medications, and cancers. Higher titers make true autoantibodies more likely, but a low-titer positive is nonspecific.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Titer is the level to which a sample can be diluted and still show a positive result; a low titer is still an interpretable result.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A positive ANA is not diagnostic of lupus by itself; low titers are nonspecific and must be interpreted in clinical context.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Malignancy is only one of several nonautoimmune causes of a positive ANA, and most low-titer positives are not due to cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ANA titer reflects how far serum can be diluted and still test positive for autoantibodies, not viral load.

questions.stem: A public health lab needs a screening test that can quantify very small amounts of a soluble antigen or antibody in patient serum, with results read as the color intensity of a solution. This is the assay used to screen donated blood for HIV. Which of the following tests best fits this description?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Agglutination assay read as visible clumping

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay

choices.label: C
choices.text: Flow cytometry of cells in suspension by laser scatter

choices.label: D
choices.text: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for nucleic acids

choices.label: E
choices.text: Western blot read as dark bands on a membrane

explanation.summary: ELISA quantifies soluble molecules with high sensitivity, reading out as color intensity, and is used to screen for HIV.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes ELISA as an assay that quantifies soluble molecules with high sensitivity, using a colorimetric substrate whose color signal is proportional to the amount of detection antibody. ELISA is specifically cited as the test used to screen for HIV before confirmatory testing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Agglutination detects the presence of antigens with low sensitivity and reads out as visible clumping, not a color-intensity quantity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Flow cytometry analyzes cells in suspension by laser scatter and fluorescence, not soluble antigen in a colorimetric well.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PCR amplifies and detects nucleic acids, not soluble proteins read by color intensity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Western blot is a qualitative test that reads out as dark bands on a membrane, not a quantitative color of solution.

questions.stem: A woman uses a home pregnancy test, which produces a colored line when the target hormone is present. Her physician notes that at-home pregnancy tests and rapid COVID-19 tests use the same lateral-flow immunoassay design, in which a capture antibody and a separate detection antibody bind different epitopes of the target. Which specific type of ELISA does this describe?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Agglutination assay

choices.label: B
choices.text: Competitive ELISA

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct ELISA

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sandwich ELISA

choices.label: E
choices.text: Western blot

explanation.summary: Lateral-flow home pregnancy and rapid COVID-19 tests are modified sandwich ELISAs.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that at-home pregnancy tests and COVID-19 tests are modified sandwich ELISAs, in which liquid flows across a membrane and a capture antibody binds the antigen while a detection antibody binds a different epitope, forming a visible line. Sandwich ELISAs are highly sensitive because the antigen is captured between two antibodies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Agglutination detects antigens by clumping red cells or particles, not by a lateral-flow antibody sandwich.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A competitive ELISA relies on competition for antibody binding, not a two-antibody sandwich flow assay.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A direct ELISA immobilizes the antigen on a plate and uses a single enzyme-linked detection antibody; it does not use a capture antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Western blot separates proteins by molecular weight and reads out as membrane bands, not a lateral-flow line.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has a positive ELISA screen for Lyme disease. To confirm the result, the lab performs a test in which proteins from the sample are separated by molecular weight using electrophoresis, transferred to a membrane, and probed with enzyme-conjugated antibodies, producing dark bands. Which test is being performed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Agglutination assay

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chromium-51 release assay

choices.label: C
choices.text: Flow cytometry

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immunofluorescence (ANA)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Western blot

explanation.summary: Western blotting separates proteins by molecular weight and detects specific proteins or antibodies as membrane bands.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes Western blot as a qualitative technique in which proteins are separated by molecular weight via electrophoresis, transferred to a membrane, and probed with an enzyme-conjugated antibody; substrate then produces dark bands indicating antibody binding. Lyme disease confirmation is listed as a clinical application.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Agglutination detects antigens by visible clumping, not by separating proteins on a gel.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A chromium-51 release assay measures cytotoxic killing of labeled target cells, not protein bands.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Flow cytometry analyzes intact cells in suspension by laser scatter and fluorescence, not electrophoretically separated proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ANA immunofluorescence localizes autoantibodies on fixed cells under a microscope; it does not separate proteins by molecular weight.

questions.stem: A laboratory runs whole blood through a flow cytometer, where cells pass single-file through a laser. One scatter parameter is proportional to a cell's size, while a second parameter is proportional to a cell's internal granularity and complexity. Which parameter reflects the internal granularity of a cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chromium-51 release

choices.label: B
choices.text: Forward scatter (FSC)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Optical density of a colorimetric substrate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Side scatter (SSC)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Titer

explanation.summary: In flow cytometry, side scatter reflects internal granularity while forward scatter reflects cell size.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that in flow cytometry a suspension of cells is hit with lasers; forward scatter (FSC) is proportional to the size of the cell, and side scatter (SSC) is proportional to the granularity of the cell. Together FSC and SSC are used to distinguish RBCs, granulocytes, monocytes, and lymphocytes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chromium-51 release measures cytotoxic killing of target cells, not a flow-cytometry scatter parameter.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Forward scatter is proportional to cell size, not internal granularity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Optical density of a colorimetric substrate is the readout of an ELISA, not a flow cytometer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Titer is a semi-quantitative measure of antibody dilution in serologic tests, unrelated to flow scatter.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old boy has had recurrent bacterial pneumonia, otitis media, and bacterial conjunctivitis. Serum testing shows low levels of all classes of immunoglobulin, and his neonatal TREC level was normal. Flow cytometry of his blood shows markedly reduced CD19-positive cells but intact CD3-positive cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic granulomatous disease

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complement C5 deficiency

choices.label: C
choices.text: DiGeorge syndrome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID)

choices.label: E
choices.text: X-linked agammaglobulinemia

explanation.summary: Absent B cells (low CD19) with intact T cells (normal CD3) and panhypogammaglobulinemia indicate X-linked agammaglobulinemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that CD19 marks total B cells and CD3 marks total T cells. A flow pattern showing low CD19-positive (and CD20-positive) B cells with intact CD3-positive T cells is characteristic of X-linked agammaglobulinemia. Loss of B cells explains the low levels of all immunoglobulin classes, and the normal neonatal TREC reflects intact T-cell development.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronic granulomatous disease is a neutrophil oxidative burst defect and would not cause absent B cells or low immunoglobulins.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Complement deficiencies do not eliminate CD19-positive B cells or cause panhypogammaglobulinemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: DiGeorge syndrome causes T-cell deficiency from thymic hypoplasia, but here T cells (CD3) are intact.
whyWrongByChoice.D: SCID shows loss of T cells (and often NK cells); this patient has intact CD3-positive T cells and a normal TREC.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to determine how many times a population of stimulated T cells has divided. She loads the cells with a membrane-permeable, initially non-fluorescent dye that becomes fluorescent and is retained inside the cell, with the amount of dye halved with each cell division. Which reagent is being used?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anti-FOXP3 antibody

choices.label: B
choices.text: Carboxyfluorescein (CFSE)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dihydrorhodamine (DHR)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phytohaemagglutinin (PHA)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Propidium iodide

explanation.summary: CFSE is a membrane-permeable dye that is halved with each division, allowing quantification of cell division.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that carboxyfluorescein (CFSE) is membrane-permeable and non-fluorescent until it penetrates the cell, where it is converted to a fluorescent dye retained inside. The amount of dye is halved with each division, allowing quantification of cell division by flow cytometry.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-FOXP3 antibody labels the transcription factor of regulatory T cells after permeabilization, not division cycles.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dihydrorhodamine is oxidized to rhodamine during the neutrophil oxidative burst; it does not track cell division.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PHA is a mitogen that stimulates lymphocyte proliferation; it is not a dye used to count divisions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Propidium iodide cannot cross an intact cell membrane and is used to assess cell viability, not division.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy has recurrent infections with catalase-positive organisms. To evaluate his neutrophils, blood is stimulated with phorbol myristate acetate (PMA) in the presence of dihydrorhodamine (DHR). In a healthy control, neutrophils oxidize DHR to fluorescent rhodamine, but the patient's neutrophils fail to do so. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic granulomatous disease

choices.label: B
choices.text: DiGeorge syndrome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Selective IgA deficiency

choices.label: D
choices.text: Severe combined immunodeficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: X-linked agammaglobulinemia

explanation.summary: Failure of PMA-stimulated neutrophils to oxidize DHR to rhodamine indicates a defective oxidative burst, seen in chronic granulomatous disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that neutrophils stimulated with PMA in the presence of DHR use reactive oxygen species from the oxidative burst to oxidize DHR to rhodamine. Deficiencies in the oxidative burst cause chronic granulomatous disease (CGD); a CGD patient's neutrophils lack this capacity, so DHR is not converted, exactly as seen here.

whyWrongByChoice.B: DiGeorge syndrome causes T-cell deficiency from thymic hypoplasia and does not affect the neutrophil oxidative burst.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Selective IgA deficiency involves reduced IgA antibody, not a defective DHR/oxidative burst response.
whyWrongByChoice.D: SCID is a combined T- and (often) NK-cell defect detected by flow cytometry, not a neutrophil oxidative burst failure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: X-linked agammaglobulinemia is a B-cell/antibody defect and does not impair the neutrophil oxidative burst.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old nurse who received the BCG (TB) vaccine as a child needs screening for latent tuberculosis. Her clinician orders an interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) instead of the tuberculin skin test. Which of the following best explains why the IGRA is preferred in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It amplifies mycobacterial DNA to quantify bacterial load

choices.label: B
choices.text: It assesses neutrophil oxidative burst against mycobacteria

choices.label: C
choices.text: It directly measures circulating antibodies against tuberculosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is less prone to false-positive results from prior TB vaccination

choices.label: E
choices.text: It requires no blood sample, only a skin reading

explanation.summary: IGRAs measure T-cell IFN-gamma release to TB-specific antigens and are less prone to false positives from BCG vaccination than the skin test.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the IGRA as an IFN-gamma release assay used to diagnose Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, in which a blood sample is exposed to TB-specific antigens so that TB-specific CD4 and CD8 T cells produce IFN-gamma. It is presented as an alternative to the TB skin test (PPD) that is less prone to false positives from TB vaccination.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IGRA is a cytokine release assay, not a nucleic acid amplification (PCR) test; it does not quantify bacterial DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IGRA assesses T-cell cytokine production, not the neutrophil oxidative burst.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IGRA measures T-cell cytokine (IFN-gamma) release, not circulating antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IGRA requires a blood sample; it is the skin test (PPD) that is read on the skin.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man presents with cough and fever for 3 days, and a chest x-ray shows lobar pneumonia. This is the third time in the past 12 months that he has been diagnosed with and treated for x-ray-documented pneumonia. His physician is concerned about an underlying immunodeficiency and plans an initial laboratory evaluation. Which of the following tests is most appropriately deferred until the results of the initial screening are available?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B- and T-cell subset analysis by flow cytometry

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complete blood count with differential and smear review

choices.label: C
choices.text: HIV screening with a fourth-generation antigen/antibody assay

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pre- and post-vaccination antibody levels to pneumococcal antigens

choices.label: E
choices.text: Quantitative immunoglobulin levels for IgG, IgA, and IgM

explanation.summary: More than two x-ray-documented pneumonias in 12 months warrants a screening immunodeficiency workup; lymphocyte subset analysis is a second-tier test guided by those results.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's case concludes that a history of more than two x-ray-documented episodes of pneumonia in 12 months is concerning for immunodeficiency. The initial evaluation should include a CBC with differential, HIV screening, quantitative immunoglobulin levels, and pre- and post-vaccination antibodies. Additional evaluation such as B- and T-cell subsets depends on the screening test results, so flow cytometric subset analysis is the test that is deferred.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A CBC with differential is part of the initial screening evaluation, not a deferred test.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HIV screening is part of the initial evaluation because HIV infection is a common cause of acquired immunodeficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pre- and post-vaccination antibody levels are part of the initial screen and assess the ability to mount specific antibody responses.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Quantitative immunoglobulin levels are an initial screening test that helps detect humoral deficiency.

questions.stem: A nurse performs bedside blood typing on a trauma patient using a kit in which anti-A, anti-B, and anti-D antibodies are fixed to separate membrane circles, with a fourth circle serving as a control. After the blood sample is added, agglutination is seen in the anti-A, anti-B, and anti-D circles and also in the control circle. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction occurring in vivo

choices.label: B
choices.text: Invalid result requiring a repeat test

choices.label: C
choices.text: Type AB negative blood in a D-negative recipient

choices.label: D
choices.text: Type AB positive blood with a valid clear control

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type O positive blood lacking both A and B antigens

explanation.summary: Agglutination in the control circle of a blood typing kit means the test is invalid, regardless of what the antigen circles show.
explanation.whyCorrect: In a blood typing kit, agglutination indicates immune complex formation between fixed antibody and an antigen on the red blood cells. The control circle contains no typing antibody and should never agglutinate; the kit's reading guide lists clumping in all four circles, including the control, as an invalid result. When the control clumps, the antigen circles cannot be interpreted and the typing must be repeated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An acute hemolytic transfusion reaction is an in vivo type II hypersensitivity reaction after incompatible transfusion, not a reading of a typing kit.
whyWrongByChoice.C: AB negative would show no agglutination in the anti-D circle, and again the control must remain clear for any interpretation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: AB positive would show agglutination in anti-A, anti-B, and anti-D circles with a clear control; a clumped control invalidates the reading.
whyWrongByChoice.E: O positive cells carry no A or B antigen and would not agglutinate in the anti-A or anti-B circles.

questions.stem: A pathologist examining a kidney biopsy from a patient with suspected autoimmune disease wants to determine where within the tissue section a target antigen is located. Which of the following techniques is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Agglutination

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chromium-51 release assay

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immunofluorescence

choices.label: E
choices.text: Western blot

explanation.summary: Immunofluorescence is the microscope-based technique that localizes target molecules within a tissue section or smear.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes immunofluorescence as a microscope-based technique used to determine the location of the target molecule(s) in a tissue section or smear, using a detection antibody labeled with a fluorophore (fluorochrome). Its listed use is detecting the location of surface-bound antigens, with results read as fluorescence in patterns.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Agglutination detects the presence of an antigen by immune complex formation in solution; it gives no information about location within tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A chromium-51 release assay quantifies cytotoxic killing of labeled target cells and is not a localization technique.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ELISA estimates the quantity of a soluble antigen by color intensity of a solution and does not localize antigens in tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Western blot separates proteins by molecular weight on a gel and shows bands on a membrane, not the position of an antigen within a tissue section.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman reports several months of dry eyes and dry mouth and has bilateral parotid gland enlargement. An antinuclear antibody test on fixed human cells shows high-titer nuclear fluorescence. Which of the following staining patterns is most strongly associated with her likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Centromere

choices.label: B
choices.text: Homogeneous

choices.label: C
choices.text: No nuclear staining

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nucleolar

choices.label: E
choices.text: Speckled

explanation.summary: A speckled ANA pattern is associated with Sjogren syndrome, the likely diagnosis in a patient with dry eyes and dry mouth.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dry eyes, dry mouth, and parotid enlargement suggest Sjogren syndrome. The brick's ANA figure pairs each immunofluorescence staining pattern with a disease association, and the speckled pattern is associated with Sjogren's. Specific patterns have known associations and help narrow the differential diagnosis and guide further testing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The centromere pattern is associated with CREST syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The homogeneous pattern is associated with systemic lupus erythematosus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The stem states that high-titer nuclear fluorescence was seen, so an absence of nuclear staining does not fit.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The nucleolar pattern is associated with scleroderma.

questions.stem: In a direct ELISA, purified antigen is immobilized in a microplate well. The well is washed before the enzyme-conjugated detection antibody is added, and washed again before the colorimetric substrate is added. Which of the following is the primary purpose of these washing steps?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activate the enzyme conjugated to the antibody

choices.label: B
choices.text: Convert the substrate into a colored product

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cross-link proteins to fix them to the plate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Denature the immobilized antigen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Remove unbound reagents from the well

explanation.summary: Washing between ELISA steps removes unbound reagents so that only bound antibody generates signal.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's direct ELISA figure notes that washing is done between steps to remove unbound reagents. Because the color signal is proportional to the amount of detection antibody, any antibody that remains in the well without being bound to antigen would falsely raise the signal; washing removes it before the substrate is added.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The enzyme is already active as part of the conjugated antibody; it acts on the substrate that is added in the final step.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The colored product is generated when the enzyme acts on the colorimetric substrate, not by the wash buffer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chemical cross-linking (fixation) is a step used for permeabilization of cells in flow cytometry, not a purpose of ELISA washes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The antigen must remain intact and affixed to the solid surface so that the detection antibody can bind it; washing is not meant to denature it.

questions.stem: A laboratory develops an assay in which a purified viral antigen is bound to the bottom of a microplate well. Patient serum is added so that any antigen-specific antibody binds as an unlabeled primary antibody. An enzyme-tagged secondary antibody directed against human immunoglobulin is then added, followed by substrate, and the color signal is read. Which of the following ELISA formats does this describe?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Competitive ELISA

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct ELISA

choices.label: C
choices.text: Indirect ELISA

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lateral flow assay

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sandwich ELISA

explanation.summary: An indirect ELISA uses bound antigen, an unlabeled primary antibody, and a tagged secondary antibody, amplifying the signal and allowing detection of antibody in serum.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's figure of ELISA types defines the indirect ELISA as bound antigen, unlabeled primary antibody, tagged secondary antibody, and then substrate, with signal relative to the amount of primary antibody. This format gives an amplified signal and allows detection of an antibody, which is why indirect ELISAs are better than direct ELISAs for detecting antibody in a patient's serum.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A competitive ELISA is listed as one of the four main types but is not the format in which a tagged anti-human immunoglobulin secondary antibody detects bound primary antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.B: In a direct ELISA the detection antibody is itself conjugated to the enzyme and binds the bound antigen; there is no separate tagged secondary antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lateral flow assays are modified sandwich ELISAs in which liquid flow carries antigen to a capture antibody on a membrane, not a well-based antigen-primary-secondary format.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A sandwich ELISA begins with an immobilized capture antibody that binds antigen from the sample, followed by a tagged detection antibody against a different epitope.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man has a positive HIV screening ELISA, which detected both antibodies to HIV and viral antigens. His physician orders additional testing. Which of the following is a primary purpose of the further testing that follows a positive HIV ELISA screen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Determine ABO and Rh blood group antigens

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enumerate CD34-positive hematopoietic stem cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Localize viral antigen within a tissue section

choices.label: D
choices.text: Measure neutrophil oxidative burst capacity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Quantify viral load and differentiate viral strains

explanation.summary: After a positive HIV ELISA screen, further tests quantify viral load, monitor treatment response, and differentiate viral strains.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that ELISAs screen for HIV by detecting both antibodies to HIV and viral antigens, and that if the ELISA screen is positive, further tests can be used to quantify viral load, monitor treatment response, and differentiate viral strains. These follow-up measures guide prognosis and management rather than simply repeating the diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blood typing by agglutination is performed for transfusion compatibility, not as HIV follow-up testing.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD34 marks hematopoietic stem cells; enumerating them is unrelated to confirming or staging HIV infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Localizing an antigen in tissue is the role of immunofluorescence and is not the follow-up to a positive HIV screen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The oxidative burst (DHR) assay evaluates neutrophil function in suspected chronic granulomatous disease, not HIV infection.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman with rapidly progressive dementia and myoclonus undergoes confirmatory testing for Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. The laboratory separates proteins from her sample by gel electrophoresis, transfers them to a membrane, probes the membrane with an enzyme-conjugated antibody, and adds substrate. Which of the following best describes the type of result this test provides?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Color intensity proportional to protein quantity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fluorescence pattern showing antigen location

choices.label: C
choices.text: Qualitative bands indicating a specific protein

choices.label: D
choices.text: Scatter plot of cell size and granularity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Visible clumping indicating antigen presence

explanation.summary: Western blot is a qualitative technique whose result is dark bands on a membrane indicating antibody binding to a specific protein.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes Western blotting as a qualitative technique for detecting a specific protein, or antibodies to a specific protein, in which proteins are separated by molecular weight, transferred to a membrane, exposed to an enzyme-conjugated antibody, and developed with substrate so that bands indicate antibody binding. Confirmation of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, a form of rapidly progressive dementia, is one of its few clinical applications, and the brick emphasizes that Western blots are not quantitative.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Color intensity of a solution proportional to quantity is the readout of an ELISA, which quantifies soluble molecules; Western blots are not quantitative.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A fluorescence pattern showing location is the result of immunofluorescence, such as an ANA test.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A scatter plot of cell size (FSC) and granularity (SSC) is generated by flow cytometry, a cell-based test.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Visible clumping (immune complex formation) is the result of an agglutination test such as blood typing.

questions.stem: A laboratory director is comparing antibody-based tests for detecting a target antigen. Which of the following tests has the lowest sensitivity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Agglutination

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay

choices.label: C
choices.text: Indirect Western blot

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sandwich ELISA

choices.label: E
choices.text: Western blot

explanation.summary: Agglutination has low sensitivity, whereas ELISA and Western blot have high sensitivity in the range of 0.1 ng.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's table of antibody-based tests lists agglutination as detecting the presence of antigen with low sensitivity, with immune complex formation as the readout. In contrast, both ELISA/EIA and Western blot are listed with high sensitivity (0.1 ng). Agglutination is therefore the least sensitive of the methods compared.

whyWrongByChoice.B: ELISA is listed with high sensitivity (0.1 ng) and quantifies soluble antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An indirect Western blot adds a detection antibody to the standard high-sensitivity Western blot; it does not have low sensitivity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sandwich ELISAs are described as highly sensitive because the antigen is captured between two antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Western blot is listed with high sensitivity (0.1 ng), reading out as dark bands on a membrane.

questions.stem: Whole blood is run through a flow cytometer and each cell is plotted by forward scatter (x-axis) and side scatter (y-axis). Four populations are seen: one clustered near the origin with low forward and side scatter, one with intermediate forward scatter and low side scatter, one with intermediate forward and side scatter, and one with high forward scatter and the highest side scatter. Which of the following cell types makes up the population with the highest side scatter?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cell debris

choices.label: B
choices.text: Granulocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lymphocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Monocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Residual red blood cells

explanation.summary: On an FSC versus SSC plot, granulocytes form the population with the highest side scatter because they are the most granular cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Side scatter is proportional to the granularity of a cell, and forward scatter to its size. The brick's flow cytometry figure shows that FSC and SSC can be used to quantify RBCs, granulocytes, monocytes, and lymphocytes in a blood sample; granulocytes occupy the region of high forward scatter and the highest side scatter, consistent with their abundant cytoplasmic granules.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Debris is found near the origin with the lowest forward and side scatter, not at the highest side scatter.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lymphocytes form the low-side-scatter population with intermediate forward scatter, reflecting small, non-granular cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Monocytes sit between lymphocytes and granulocytes, with intermediate forward and side scatter.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Residual red blood cells cluster with debris near the origin, with low forward and side scatter.

questions.stem: A flow cytometry panel uses a fluorophore-conjugated antibody directed against a cell-surface protein that functions as the co-receptor for MHC class I. Which of the following cell populations does this antibody identify?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytotoxic T cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Helper T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Macrophages

choices.label: E
choices.text: Natural killer cells

explanation.summary: CD8, the co-receptor for MHC class I, is the marker for cytotoxic T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's table of high-yield CD markers lists CD8 as the marker for cytotoxic T cells, with the protein function of co-receptor for MHC I. Fluorophore-conjugated antibodies against CD4 and CD8 allow helper T cells and cytotoxic T cells to be differentiated by flow cytometry.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B cells are marked by CD19 and CD20, which are involved in B cell development and activation rather than MHC co-recognition.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Helper T cells are marked by CD4, which functions as the co-receptor for MHC class II, not class I.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Macrophages are marked by CD14, a receptor for PAMPs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Natural killer cells are marked by CD16 (an Fc-gamma receptor involved in ADCC) and CD56, not an MHC co-receptor.

questions.stem: A researcher isolates natural killer cells from a blood sample by flow cytometry using a fluorophore-conjugated antibody against CD16. Which of the following best describes the function of the CD16 protein?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Co-receptor that binds MHC class II on antigen-presenting cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fc-gamma receptor involved in antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ligand that activates B cells and macrophages by binding CD40

choices.label: D
choices.text: Receptor for pathogen-associated molecular patterns on macrophages

choices.label: E
choices.text: Signal-transducing component of the T cell receptor complex

explanation.summary: CD16 is the NK cell marker that functions as an Fc-gamma receptor mediating ADCC.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's CD marker table lists CD16 as a marker for NK cells with the protein function of an Fc-gamma receptor (FcyR) involved in antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC). CD56 is listed as a possible NK marker with unclear function, so CD16/56 together are used to identify NK cells on flow plots.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The co-receptor for MHC class II is CD4, the helper T cell marker.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The ligand that activates B cells, macrophages, and endothelial cells by binding CD40 is CD154 (CD40L), a marker of activated CD4 T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The receptor for PAMPs listed in the table is CD14, the macrophage marker.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The component of the TCR complex involved in signal transduction is CD3, the total T cell marker.

questions.stem: Lymphocytes from a 5-year-old boy with recurrent infections are stimulated in culture, and flow cytometry is used to determine whether his CD4-positive T cells can become activated. Which of the following surface markers is the most appropriate indicator of activated CD4-positive T cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD3

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD8

choices.label: C
choices.text: CD16

choices.label: D
choices.text: CD19

choices.label: E
choices.text: CD154

explanation.summary: CD154 (CD40L) is the marker for activated CD4-positive T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's CD marker table lists CD154 (CD40L) as the marker for activated CD4+ T cells. Its protein function is to activate B cells, macrophages, and endothelial cells after CD40 binds to CD40L, so its appearance on the surface after stimulation indicates that helper T cells have become activated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD3 is a marker for total T cells, present on resting and activated cells alike, so it cannot distinguish activation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD8 marks cytotoxic T cells and is present regardless of activation state; it does not indicate helper T cell activation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD16 is an NK cell marker (Fc-gamma receptor involved in ADCC) and is not an activation marker of CD4 T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CD19 marks total B cells, not T cells.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to identify macrophages in a cell suspension by flow cytometry using a fluorophore-conjugated antibody against a surface protein that acts as a receptor for pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs). Which of the following markers should be targeted?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD3

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD14

choices.label: C
choices.text: CD19

choices.label: D
choices.text: CD34

choices.label: E
choices.text: CD56

explanation.summary: CD14 is the macrophage marker and functions as a receptor for PAMPs.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's CD marker table lists CD14 as the marker for macrophages with the protein function of receptor for PAMPs. Fluorophore-conjugated antibodies directed to such cell-surface markers allow specific cell types to be distinguished by flow cytometry.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD3 marks total T cells and is part of the TCR complex involved in signal transduction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD19 marks total B cells and is involved in B cell development, activation, and differentiation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CD34 marks hematopoietic stem cells, not macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CD56 is a possible marker for NK cells with unclear function.

questions.stem: A 2-month-old boy has a positive newborn screen with very low T cell receptor excision circles. Flow cytometry of his lymphocytes shows CD19-positive cells making up 95% of lymphocytes, CD3-positive cells less than 1%, and CD16/56-positive cells 2%. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autosomal SCID with absent B cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic granulomatous disease (neutrophil defect)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Selective IgA deficiency (antibody defect)

choices.label: D
choices.text: X-linked agammaglobulinemia (B cell defect)

choices.label: E
choices.text: X-linked SCID (gamma chain mutation)

explanation.summary: Loss of T cells and NK cells with preserved (proportionally expanded) B cells is the flow cytometry signature of X-linked SCID.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's flow cytometry example shows a patient with X-linked SCID due to a common gamma chain (cy) mutation, a type of SCID that results in loss of T cells and NK cells. The patient's plots show B = 96%, T < 1%, and NK = 2%, whereas the healthy control has signals for CD19, CD3, and CD16/56 in their respective quadrants. The very low TREC count reflects absent T cell production, consistent with a T cell maturation disorder.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick notes that autosomal SCID would have no B cells; this patient's lymphocytes are almost entirely B cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic granulomatous disease is a neutrophil oxidative burst defect detected by the DHR assay; lymphocyte subsets are preserved.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Selective IgA deficiency is an antibody isotype deficiency and does not eliminate T cells and NK cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: X-linked agammaglobulinemia shows the opposite pattern: low CD19/CD20 B cells with intact CD3 T cells, and TRECs are normal.

questions.stem: A researcher treats a tumor cell line with a new chemotherapeutic agent, then adds propidium iodide and analyzes the cells by flow cytometry. A large fraction of the treated cells show strong propidium iodide fluorescence, whereas untreated cells do not. Which of the following best explains the fluorescence in the treated cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cellular enzymes converted the dye into fluorescent CFSE

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of membrane integrity let the dye reach DNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reactive oxygen species oxidized the dye to rhodamine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Successive cell divisions diluted the dye by half

choices.label: E
choices.text: Surface Fc receptors captured the dye on the cell membrane

explanation.summary: Propidium iodide cannot cross an intact membrane, so fluorescence marks cells whose membrane integrity has been lost.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that propidium iodide cannot cross a cell membrane and increases in fluorescence when bound to DNA. It is used to evaluate cell viability (necrotic, apoptotic, and healthy cells) based on membrane integrity. Treated cells that fluoresce have compromised membranes that allowed the dye to enter and bind DNA, indicating that the drug killed them.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Carboxyfluorescein is the membrane-permeable compound converted intracellularly to CFSE; propidium iodide is not converted this way.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxidation to fluorescent rhodamine describes dihydrorhodamine in the neutrophil oxidative burst assay.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Halving of dye with each division describes CFSE, which is used to quantify cell division, not propidium iodide.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Propidium iodide fluoresces when bound to DNA inside the cell, not when held at the surface by receptors.

questions.stem: A laboratory wants to quantify regulatory T cells in a blood sample by flow cytometry using a fluorophore-conjugated antibody against the transcription factor FOXP3. Which of the following steps is required before the anti-FOXP3 antibody can label the cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fixation and detergent permeabilization

choices.label: B
choices.text: Incubation with pokeweed mitogen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Labeling the cells with chromium-51

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loading the cells with carboxyfluorescein

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stimulation with phorbol myristate acetate

explanation.summary: Intracellular targets such as the transcription factor FOXP3 require fixation and permeabilization so antibodies can enter the cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that cells can be fixed (proteins chemically cross-linked) and treated with detergents to remove all lipids, making them permeable to antibodies. Antibodies can then label intracellular molecules such as cytokines in vesicles, granule contents, and transcription factors. FOXP3 is the critical transcription factor that distinguishes regulatory T cells from other CD4 T cells, so permeabilization is required before staining.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Pokeweed mitogen polyclonally stimulates T and B cells in stimulation assays; it does not permeabilize cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chromium-51 labels target cells in cytotoxicity assays and is unrelated to intracellular antibody staining.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Carboxyfluorescein (CFSE) is a dye used to quantify cell division, not a step that permits antibody access to intracellular proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PMA is a protein kinase C activator used to stimulate neutrophils in the DHR oxidative burst assay; it does not make cells permeable to antibodies.

questions.stem: A laboratory evaluating an infant's lymphocyte function wants to use a single plant-derived mitogen that polyclonally stimulates both T cells and B cells, regardless of receptor specificity. Which of the following should be used?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Concanavalin A (ConA), a plant mitogen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Phorbol myristate acetate (PMA)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phytohemagglutinin (PHA), a plant mitogen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pokeweed mitogen (PWM)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tetanus toxin antigen

explanation.summary: Pokeweed mitogen stimulates both T and B cells, whereas PHA and ConA predominantly activate T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines mitogens as plant-derived compounds that polyclonally stimulate lymphocytes regardless of TCR or BCR specificity. Of the three most used mitogens, PHA and ConA predominantly activate T cells, while PWM stimulates both T and B cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ConA, like PHA, predominantly activates T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: PMA is a protein kinase C activator used to stimulate the neutrophil oxidative burst; it is not a plant-derived lymphocyte mitogen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PHA predominantly activates T cells, so it would not assess B cell responses.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tetanus toxin is used for antigen-specific stimulation of lymphocytes in immunized individuals, not polyclonal stimulation.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with X-linked agammaglobulinemia (absent B cells, intact T cells, low immunoglobulins of all classes) has his lymphocytes stimulated with phytohemagglutinin and concanavalin A, with proliferation measured by CFSE dilution. Which of the following results is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absent proliferation because PHA acts only on B cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Absent proliferation from a defective oxidative burst

choices.label: C
choices.text: Exaggerated proliferation from loss of regulatory T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Normal or only partially reduced proliferation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Severely reduced proliferation from T cell lymphopenia

explanation.summary: Severely reduced mitogen responses reflect decreased T cell numbers; patients with humoral deficiency show partial or normal responses.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that severely reduced mitogen responses may indicate conditions like SCID, profound T cell lymphopenia, or advanced HIV infection due to a decreased number of T cells. In contrast, patients with humoral deficiency or milder syndromes of combined deficiency might exhibit partial or normal responses. X-linked agammaglobulinemia is a humoral deficiency with intact T cells, and PHA and ConA predominantly activate T cells, so proliferation is expected to be normal or only partially reduced.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PHA and ConA predominantly activate T cells, not B cells, so absent B cells do not abolish the response.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The oxidative burst is a neutrophil function evaluated with the DHR assay; it does not determine lymphocyte proliferation to mitogens.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nothing in X-linked agammaglobulinemia removes regulatory T cells, and the brick does not describe exaggerated mitogen responses in humoral deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: T cell lymphopenia is the cause of severely reduced responses in SCID or advanced HIV, but this patient has intact T cells.

questions.stem: A researcher studying tumor immunity wants to quantify the ability of a patient's natural killer cells to kill tumor target cells. Which of the following assays is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CFSE dilution assay

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chromium-51 release assay

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dihydrorhodamine oxidative burst assay

choices.label: D
choices.text: Interferon-gamma release assay

choices.label: E
choices.text: TREC quantification by PCR

explanation.summary: Chromium-51 release assays quantify the cytotoxic ability of CTLs or NK cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that chromium-51 (51Cr) release assays are used to quantify the cytotoxic ability of CTLs or NK cells, particularly in the study of tumor and viral immunity. Target cells are labeled with 51Cr; if they are killed, 51Cr is released into the solution, and the activity (radiation level) is counted in a gamma counter or liquid scintillation counter.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CFSE dilution quantifies cell division, not the cytotoxic killing of target cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The DHR assay measures the neutrophil oxidative burst and is used to diagnose chronic granulomatous disease, not NK cytotoxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An IGRA measures IFN-gamma released by TB-specific T cells and is used to diagnose Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TREC quantification assesses T cell production in neonatal screening and does not measure killing of target cells.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl whose parents declined all childhood vaccinations is evaluated for possible immunodeficiency because of recurrent infections. Her lymphocytes proliferate and produce cytokines normally in response to phytohemagglutinin and to Candida antigen but show no response to tetanus toxin antigen. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absent tetanus response reflects lack of prior immunization

choices.label: B
choices.text: Generalized T cell activation defect affecting mitogen responses

choices.label: C
choices.text: Impaired memory against environmental yeast such as Candida

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neutrophil oxidative burst deficiency detected by DHR testing

choices.label: E
choices.text: T cell maturation defect limited to tetanus-specific cells in the thymus

explanation.summary: Antigen-specific responses to tetanus toxin are expected only in immunized individuals, so an absent response in an unvaccinated child does not indicate a T cell defect.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that antigen stimulation assesses cytokine production and/or proliferation in response to specific antigens, using proteins from Candida (an environmental yeast almost all people have memory against) and/or tetanus toxin (most people are immunized against this toxin). It further states that T cells should produce cytokines upon stimulation with mitogens or tetanus antigen if the person is vaccinated. Her normal responses to PHA and Candida show that T cell activation is intact; the absent tetanus response is explained by her never having been immunized.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A generalized activation defect would produce low or absent cytokine responses to mitogens as well, but her PHA response is normal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Her lymphocytes responded normally to Candida antigen, so memory against the environmental yeast is intact.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The oxidative burst is a neutrophil function tested with DHR and PMA, not with lymphocyte antigen stimulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A maturation defect would not selectively eliminate tetanus-specific cells while preserving Candida-specific memory; the missing tetanus memory is due to no vaccination.

questions.stem: A newborn's dried blood spot screen shows very low levels of T cell receptor excision circles (TRECs). Which of the following does this result most directly suggest?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Impaired B cell maturation (e.g., X-linked agammaglobulinemia)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Impaired kappa light chain recombination in developing B cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Impaired neutrophil oxidative burst (e.g., chronic granulomatous disease)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Impaired NK cell cytotoxicity against virus-infected cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Impaired T cell maturation (e.g., SCID or DiGeorge syndrome)

explanation.summary: TRECs are byproducts of V(D)J recombination in TCR development, so a low count indicates a T cell maturation disorder.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes TRECs as small, circular DNA fragments formed during V(D)J recombination in TCR development. In neonatal TREC screening, the amount of TRECs in umbilical cord or peripheral blood is quantified by PCR, and a low TREC count indicates a T cell maturation disorder. Patients with low TREC levels might have SCID or DiGeorge syndrome, and TREC analysis is a standard component of newborn screening in all states.

whyWrongByChoice.A: TRECs reflect TCR, not BCR, development; X-linked agammaglobulinemia has normal TRECs because T cell development is intact.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Kappa light chain recombination is assessed by KRECs (kappa-deleting recombination circles), a separate and much less commonly used test of BCR development.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The neutrophil oxidative burst is assessed with the DHR assay, not by TREC counts.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NK cell cytotoxicity is quantified with a chromium-51 release assay, and TRECs do not report on NK function.

questions.stem: A researcher studying a patient with a suspected interferonopathy wants to assess type 1 interferon activity in the patient's blood but finds that type 1 IFN itself is difficult to measure directly. Which of the following is the most appropriate approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Measure transcription of interferon-stimulated genes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Perform an interferon-gamma release assay

choices.label: C
choices.text: Quantify cytotoxicity with a chromium-51 release assay

choices.label: D
choices.text: Quantify T cell receptor excision circles by PCR

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stain for intracellular IL-10 after permeabilization

explanation.summary: When type 1 IFN is hard to measure directly, its transcriptional response (IFN-stimulated genes) is measured instead.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that some portions of the immune response are difficult to measure directly, using type 1 IFN as the example. Instead of directly measuring type 1 IFN, the transcriptional responses it induces, called IFN-stimulated genes, are measured. This is a nucleic acid-based approach, building on PCR's ability to quantify gene expression.

whyWrongByChoice.B: An IGRA measures IFN-gamma released by TB-specific T cells, a different cytokine used to diagnose tuberculosis infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A chromium-51 release assay quantifies killing of target cells by CTLs or NK cells, not interferon signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TREC quantification assesses T cell production during development and says nothing about type 1 IFN activity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Intracellular IL-10 staining measures a different cytokine in permeabilized cells and does not report type 1 IFN activity.

questions.stem: A 9-month-old boy has flow cytometry and functional assays indicating a T cell deficiency, but the specific inborn error of immunity responsible remains undetermined. Which of the following is most appropriate to establish a definitive diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Measuring serum ANA titer and staining pattern

choices.label: B
choices.text: Performing a chromium-51 release assay

choices.label: C
choices.text: Quantifying lymphocyte proliferation to pokeweed mitogen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Repeating the dihydrorhodamine oxidative burst assay

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sequencing a targeted panel of candidate genes

explanation.summary: Definitive diagnosis of a specific inborn error of immunity requires identifying the causative mutation by gene sequencing.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that all of the antibody-, cell-, and nucleic acid-based tests discussed help determine which portion of the immune system is deficient, but definitive diagnosis of a specific inborn error of immunity (IEI) often requires determining what mutation(s) are present. Early methods used single-gene sequencing; now DNA samples are often tested by a target gene panel of multiple genes, whole exome sequencing (all protein-encoding genes), or even whole-genome sequencing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ANA testing screens for autoimmunity by immunofluorescence and cannot define a genetic immunodeficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A chromium-51 release assay quantifies cytotoxic function and does not determine which mutation is present.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mitogen stimulation is a functional assay that helps localize the deficiency to T cells but does not identify the specific genetic cause.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The DHR assay evaluates the neutrophil oxidative burst for chronic granulomatous disease; it does not identify the mutation behind a T cell deficiency.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has been taking prednisone for several weeks. A routine complete blood count shows an elevated white blood cell count with a predominance of neutrophils. She is afebrile and has no cough, dysuria, or other localizing signs of infection. Which of the following best explains her elevated white blood cell count?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A new bacterial infection stimulating neutrophil release

choices.label: B
choices.text: Impaired apoptosis of circulating lymphocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased proliferation of myeloid precursors in the bone marrow

choices.label: D
choices.text: Redistribution of eosinophils into the peripheral blood

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced neutrophil margination

explanation.summary: Glucocorticoids reduce leukocyte margination, producing an artificial neutrophil-predominant leukocytosis that can be mistaken for infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glucocorticoids reduce white blood cell margination, so neutrophils that would normally adhere to vessel walls remain free in the bloodstream. The result is an artificial (demargination) leukocytosis with a predominance of neutrophils. The brick notes this elevation has misled many providers into suspecting a new or worsening infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: She is afebrile with no localizing signs; the leukocytosis is a predictable drug effect rather than evidence of infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucocorticoids actually promote T-cell apoptosis and lower lymphocyte counts; the increase here is in neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The rise reflects demargination of existing neutrophils into circulation, not increased bone marrow production.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The predominant cells are neutrophils, not eosinophils, and glucocorticoids tend to reduce eosinophils.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with a severe asthma exacerbation is treated with a glucocorticoid, which reduces production of inflammatory cytokines. Inhibition of which of the following is chiefly responsible for this anti-inflammatory effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dihydrofolate reductase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase

choices.label: C
choices.text: mTOR

choices.label: D
choices.text: NF-kB

choices.label: E
choices.text: NFAT (nuclear factor of activated T cells)

explanation.summary: Glucocorticoids inhibit NF-kB, a key transcription factor for inflammatory cytokine production.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that glucocorticoids inhibit the protein NF-kB, a transcription factor that drives cytokine production, along with other secondary pathways that lead to inflammation. Blocking NF-kB lowers inflammatory cytokine output and suppresses both B- and T-cell function.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dihydrofolate reductase is inhibited by methotrexate, a cytostatic agent.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase is inhibited by mycophenolate, not by glucocorticoids.
whyWrongByChoice.C: mTOR is a kinase inhibited by sirolimus, not by glucocorticoids.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NFAT is the transcription factor dephosphorylated by calcineurin; it is the target of calcineurin inhibitors, not glucocorticoids.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has taken high-dose glucocorticoids for more than a year. She has developed a rounded 'moon' face, a dorsocervical fat pad, central obesity, thin skin with easy bruising, and proximal muscle weakness. Which of the following best describes this constellation of findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemorrhagic cystitis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iatrogenic hypercortisolism

choices.label: D
choices.text: Myelosuppression from a cytostatic agent

choices.label: E
choices.text: Opportunistic viral infection

explanation.summary: Chronic glucocorticoid use can cause hypercortisolism (Cushing syndrome) with characteristic fat redistribution and tissue changes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that glucocorticoid use may lead to hypercortisolism (Cushing syndrome), characterized by a dorsocervical fat pad ('buffalo hump'), central obesity, peripheral muscle wasting, bone loss, and 'moon' facies. This patient's findings match iatrogenic Cushing syndrome from prolonged high-dose steroids.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nephrotoxicity is the hallmark toxicity of calcineurin inhibitors and would present with rising creatinine, not fat redistribution.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemorrhagic cystitis is a bladder toxicity of cyclophosphamide and would present with dysuria and hematuria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Myelosuppression from cytostatic agents causes low blood counts, not the described body-habitus changes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An opportunistic infection would present with infectious signs, not the classic Cushingoid appearance.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis that remains inadequately controlled is started on methotrexate. By inhibiting which of the following enzymes does methotrexate reduce nucleotide synthesis and lymphocyte proliferation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Calcineurin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dihydrofolate reductase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase

choices.label: D
choices.text: mTOR

choices.label: E
choices.text: PRPP amidotransferase

explanation.summary: Methotrexate is a folic acid analog that competitively inhibits dihydrofolate reductase.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes methotrexate as a folic acid analog that competitively inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), an enzyme crucial for nucleic acid production. By lowering nucleotides, specifically thymidine, methotrexate interferes with DNA synthesis and inhibits lymphocyte proliferation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Calcineurin is inhibited by tacrolimus and cyclosporine, not methotrexate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase is the target of mycophenolate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: mTOR is inhibited by sirolimus, not methotrexate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PRPP amidotransferase is blocked by the azathioprine metabolite 6-mercaptopurine, not by methotrexate.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man receiving cyclophosphamide for non-Hodgkin lymphoma develops dysuria and gross hematuria. Which of the following best explains this adverse effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow suppression causing thrombocytopenia within 7 to 10 days

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cross-reactivity with renal tubular calcineurin phosphatase activity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fungal cystitis due to immunosuppression from chemotherapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nephrotoxicity from calcineurin inhibition raising serum creatinine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Toxic damage to the rapidly dividing cells of the bladder

explanation.summary: Cyclophosphamide, like other cytostatic agents, damages rapidly dividing cells, including those of the bladder.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that cytostatic agents damage rapidly dividing cells beyond the immune system, specifically naming the bladder as a target of cyclophosphamide. This bladder toxicity produces dysuria and hematuria (hemorrhagic cystitis).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Marrow suppression is a class effect of cytostatic agents but does not explain the localized dysuria pointing to the bladder.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cyclophosphamide cross-links DNA; it does not act on calcineurin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nothing in the vignette suggests a fungal infection; the presentation reflects direct drug toxicity to the bladder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nephrotoxicity is characteristic of calcineurin inhibitors, not cyclophosphamide, and would present with rising creatinine rather than localized bladder symptoms.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus is started on azathioprine. This drug is a prodrug that is converted in tissues to an active metabolite that disrupts purine nucleotide synthesis. Which of the following is that active metabolite?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 6-mercaptopurine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cortisol

choices.label: C
choices.text: Folinic acid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mycophenolic acid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rapamycin

explanation.summary: Azathioprine is a prodrug converted to 6-mercaptopurine, which blocks purine nucleotide synthesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that azathioprine is a prodrug of 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP); tissues convert it to 6-MP, which disrupts purine nucleotide synthesis by blocking PRPP amidotransferase. This blocks purine synthesis and inhibits lymphocyte proliferation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cortisol is a glucocorticoid, unrelated to azathioprine metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Folinic acid (leucovorin) is used to rescue cells from antifolate effects; it is not an azathioprine metabolite.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mycophenolic acid is the active form of mycophenolate, a different cytostatic agent that inhibits IMP dehydrogenase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rapamycin is another name for sirolimus, the mTOR inhibitor, not a metabolite of azathioprine.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man who received a kidney transplant is maintained on mycophenolate. Which of the following enzymes does mycophenolate reversibly inhibit to reduce purine synthesis and DNA replication in B and T cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Calcineurin, a serine/threonine phosphatase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dihydrofolate reductase, a folate-cycle enzyme

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inosine-5-monophosphate dehydrogenase

choices.label: D
choices.text: mTOR, a serine/threonine protein kinase

choices.label: E
choices.text: NF-kB, an inflammatory transcription factor

explanation.summary: Mycophenolate reversibly inhibits inosine-5-monophosphate dehydrogenase, reducing purine synthesis in B and T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that mycophenolate reversibly inhibits inosine-5-monophosphate (IMP) dehydrogenase, an enzyme in purine synthesis. With this enzyme inhibited, purine synthesis and DNA replication in B and T cells are reduced. It is used in organ transplantation and some autoimmune diseases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Calcineurin is inhibited by tacrolimus and cyclosporine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dihydrofolate reductase is the target of methotrexate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: mTOR is inhibited by sirolimus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NF-kB is inhibited by glucocorticoids, not mycophenolate.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman who underwent liver transplantation is started on tacrolimus to prevent rejection. Which of the following best describes its mechanism of action?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binds cyclophilin and inhibits calcineurin, decreasing IL-2 production

choices.label: B
choices.text: Binds FKBP and inhibits calcineurin, decreasing IL-2 production

choices.label: C
choices.text: Binds FKBP and inhibits mTOR, blocking the response to IL-2

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cross-links DNA, suppressing DNA replication

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibits NF-kB, reducing inflammatory cytokine production

explanation.summary: Tacrolimus binds FKBP and inhibits calcineurin, lowering IL-2 and reducing T-cell proliferation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that tacrolimus binds FK506-binding protein (FKBP); the drug-protein complex then inhibits calcineurin. Blocking calcineurin prevents dephosphorylation of NFAT, decreasing IL-2 production and reducing T-cell proliferation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Binding cyclophilin describes cyclosporine, not tacrolimus, even though both ultimately inhibit calcineurin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Binding FKBP and inhibiting mTOR describes sirolimus, which blocks the response to IL-2 rather than its production.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cross-linking DNA is the mechanism of cyclophosphamide, a cytostatic agent.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inhibiting NF-kB is the mechanism of glucocorticoids, not tacrolimus.

questions.stem: A patient with a renal transplant is treated with cyclosporine. Cyclosporine and tacrolimus both ultimately inhibit calcineurin, but they first bind different intracellular immunophilins. To which of the following does cyclosporine bind?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Calcineurin directly, without an immunophilin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cyclophilin

choices.label: C
choices.text: FK506-binding protein (FKBP)

choices.label: D
choices.text: mTOR

choices.label: E
choices.text: NFAT

explanation.summary: Cyclosporine binds cyclophilin, whereas tacrolimus binds FKBP; both complexes then inhibit calcineurin.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that tacrolimus binds FKBP while cyclosporine binds cyclophilin. In both cases, the drug binds its immunophilin, and the resulting complex inhibits calcineurin, decreasing IL-2 production.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Calcineurin inhibitors do not bind calcineurin directly; they first bind an immunophilin, and the complex then inhibits calcineurin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FK506-binding protein is bound by tacrolimus (and by sirolimus), not by cyclosporine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: mTOR is the target of sirolimus and is not the immunophilin bound by cyclosporine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NFAT is the downstream transcription factor whose activation is blocked, not the immunophilin the drug binds.

questions.stem: A transplant patient is switched to sirolimus (rapamycin). Unlike the calcineurin inhibitors, which decrease IL-2 production, sirolimus limits T-cell proliferation by which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding cyclophilin and inhibiting calcineurin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Binding FKBP and inhibiting mTOR

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cross-linking DNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Preventing the dephosphorylation of NFAT

explanation.summary: Sirolimus binds FKBP and inhibits mTOR, blocking the response to IL-2 rather than its production.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that sirolimus binds FKBP (the same protein bound by tacrolimus) and inhibits the mTOR signaling pathway. Because mTOR is a kinase important for cell survival and proliferation, its inhibition blocks T-cell proliferation and decreases antibody production by hindering the response to IL-2, as opposed to preventing production of IL-2.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Binding cyclophilin and inhibiting calcineurin describes cyclosporine, which lowers IL-2 production.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cross-linking DNA is the mechanism of cyclophosphamide.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase is the mechanism of methotrexate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Blocking dephosphorylation of NFAT is how calcineurin inhibitors reduce IL-2 production, not the mTOR mechanism.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man on tacrolimus after kidney transplantation is monitored with serial serum creatinine measurements. Which of the following adverse effects is this monitoring primarily intended to detect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cushing syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemorrhagic cystitis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hepatotoxicity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Myelosuppression

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nephrotoxicity

explanation.summary: Calcineurin inhibitors are highly nephrotoxic, so serum creatinine is monitored to detect acute renal injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation states that calcineurin inhibitors are highly nephrotoxic and that serum creatinine must be monitored closely to guard against acute renal injury. Serial creatinine measurements track kidney function in a patient on tacrolimus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cushing syndrome results from chronic glucocorticoid use, not tacrolimus, and is not tracked with creatinine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemorrhagic cystitis is a bladder toxicity of cyclophosphamide and would be assessed by urinalysis, not creatinine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepatotoxicity is more characteristic of methotrexate and would be followed with liver enzymes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Myelosuppression is a cytostatic-agent effect monitored with blood counts, not serum creatinine.

questions.stem: A physician counsels a patient who is beginning long-term immunosuppressive therapy about the risks. Which of the following is the most common adverse effect of immunosuppressive therapy in general?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cushing syndrome in all patients

choices.label: B
choices.text: Development of a new autoimmune disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased susceptibility to infections

choices.label: D
choices.text: Malignancy as the single most common effect

choices.label: E
choices.text: Permanent loss of immunologic memory

explanation.summary: By suppressing the immune system, immunosuppressants most commonly increase susceptibility to infections.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick emphasizes that suppressing the immune system leaves patients vulnerable to viral, bacterial, and fungal infections, and that the most common side effect of these medications is an elevated risk of infections. This is why monitoring patient responses is very important.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cushing syndrome is a specific consequence of chronic glucocorticoid use, not a universal effect of all immunosuppressants.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Immunosuppressants are used to treat autoimmune disease; they do not commonly cause new autoimmune disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immunosuppressants do raise cancer risk, but the brick specifies that increased infection is the most common side effect, not malignancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Immunosuppression attenuates immune responses but does not cause permanent, universal loss of immunologic memory.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man sustains a spinal cord injury in a motor vehicle collision. Within hours of the injury, his physician prescribes an immunosuppressant to manage inflammation at the injury site. Which of the following general categories of indication for immunosuppressive therapy does this scenario represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute inflammatory condition

choices.label: B
