choices.text: Autoimmune disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prevention of transplant rejection

choices.label: D
choices.text: Primary immunodeficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: White blood cell cancer

explanation.summary: Spinal cord injury is the brick's example of an acute inflammatory condition that may be treated with immunosuppressants.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists four groups of patients who may benefit from immunosuppressants: transplant recipients, patients with autoimmune diseases, patients with acute inflammatory conditions, and patients with certain WBC cancers. Spinal cord injury is given specifically as an example of an acute inflammatory condition in which immunosuppressants may be prescribed to manage inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Autoimmune diseases such as RA, IBD, MS, and SLE involve the immune system targeting the body; a traumatic spinal cord injury is not an autoimmune process.
whyWrongByChoice.C: No organ or bone marrow transplant is involved, so rejection prophylaxis does not apply.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Primary immunodeficiency is not among the brick's indications for immunosuppressants, and suppressing an already deficient immune system would not be the goal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The patient has no malignancy; WBC cancers such as leukemia and lymphoma form a separate indication category.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man receives a deceased-donor kidney transplant and is started on an immunosuppressive regimen. At discharge he asks how long he will need to take these medications. Which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: For 1 year, after which the graft is fully tolerated and drugs can stop

choices.label: B
choices.text: For the rest of his life, to prevent rejection of the graft

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only during episodes of acute rejection, then tapered off

choices.label: D
choices.text: Until his serum creatinine returns to normal and stays stable

choices.label: E
choices.text: Until his white blood cell count normalizes after induction

explanation.summary: Transplant recipients often require lifelong immunosuppression to prevent transplant rejection.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that recipients of organ and bone marrow transplants often require lifelong immunosuppression to prevent transplant rejection. The immune system continues to recognize the graft as foreign, so ongoing suppression is needed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick describes immunosuppression in transplant recipients as lifelong, not limited to a fixed period after which the graft is tolerated.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immunosuppressants are used to prevent rejection, not merely to treat it once it occurs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Normalization of creatinine indicates graft function, not that immunosuppression can be stopped; ongoing suppression is required to keep the graft from being rejected.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The WBC count is not the endpoint that determines the duration of therapy; suppression must continue as long as the graft is present.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman with an asthma exacerbation is treated with a glucocorticoid. Among its many effects, the drug reduces tissue inflammation by impairing the ability of white blood cells to migrate into tissues. Which of the following general mechanisms of immunosuppressive action does this effect represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockade of the cellular response to IL-2

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blockade of the dephosphorylation of NFAT

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibition of DNA replication in WBCs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibition of the entry of WBCs into tissues

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibition of the proliferation of WBCs

explanation.summary: Impairing WBC migration into tissues is the brick's general mechanism of inhibiting WBC entry into tissues.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists four general mechanisms of immunosuppressants: inhibiting WBC proliferation, inhibiting the entry of WBCs into tissues, inhibiting the inflammatory response, and suppressing WBC effector responses. Glucocorticoids can impair the ability of WBCs to migrate into tissues, resulting in reduced tissue inflammation, which is an example of inhibiting WBC entry into tissues.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blocking the response to IL-2 is the mechanism of sirolimus, which limits T-cell proliferation rather than migration.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Preventing NFAT dephosphorylation describes calcineurin inhibitors and reduces IL-2 production; it does not describe reduced WBC migration.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inhibiting DNA replication is the mechanism of cytostatic agents, not the migration effect of glucocorticoids.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inhibiting proliferation reduces the number of WBCs; the effect described here is a failure of existing WBCs to reach tissues.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man with a flare of asthma is given dexamethasone. This medication mimics the effects of corticosteroids that are normally produced by which of the following organs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adrenal glands

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anterior pituitary

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bone marrow

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pancreas

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thyroid gland

explanation.summary: Glucocorticoids such as dexamethasone mimic the corticosteroids produced by the adrenal glands.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that glucocorticoids mimic the effects of corticosteroids produced by the adrenal glands. The class includes prednisone, cortisol (hydrocortisone), cortisone, dexamethasone, and others, recognizable by names ending in -sone or -sol. The summary describes these drugs as mimicking endogenous steroids to reduce inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The anterior pituitary is not the source of corticosteroids; the brick attributes corticosteroid production to the adrenal glands.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bone marrow produces blood cells, including the WBCs that immunosuppressants target, not corticosteroids.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The pancreas produces digestive enzymes and hormones such as insulin, not corticosteroids.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The thyroid gland produces thyroid hormones, not the corticosteroids that glucocorticoids mimic.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman has been taking prednisone for 4 months for an autoimmune disease. A lymphocyte subset analysis shows a reduced number of circulating T cells. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blocked purine synthesis halting T-cell DNA replication

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cross-linking of DNA in proliferating T cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased cytokine production leading to T-cell apoptosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Failure of NFAT dephosphorylation reducing IL-2 transcription

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibition of mTOR preventing the response to IL-2

explanation.summary: Glucocorticoids decrease cytokine production, which eventually leads to T-cell apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that glucocorticoids suppress both B- and T-cell function and decrease cytokine production, and that this decreased cytokine production eventually leads to T-cell apoptosis. A fall in circulating T cells during prolonged prednisone therapy reflects this mechanism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blocking purine synthesis is the mechanism of azathioprine and mycophenolate, not of glucocorticoids.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DNA cross-linking is the mechanism of cyclophosphamide, a cytostatic agent, not prednisone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Preventing NFAT dephosphorylation is the mechanism of calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus and cyclosporine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inhibition of mTOR is how sirolimus limits T-cell proliferation; prednisone does not act on mTOR.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man is being treated for a hematologic malignancy, and a glucocorticoid is included in his regimen. Glucocorticoids are indicated in which of the following malignancies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hepatocellular carcinoma (hepatoma)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lung adenocarcinoma (non-small cell)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Malignant melanoma of the skin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Renal cell carcinoma (clear cell type)

explanation.summary: Glucocorticoid indications extend to certain malignancies, specifically chronic lymphocytic leukemia and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists glucocorticoid indications ranging from prolonged inflammation (such as tendonitis) to spinal cord injuries, asthma, autoimmune and autoinflammatory diseases, and even certain malignancies such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia and non-Hodgkin lymphoma. These are white blood cell cancers, one of the four general indication categories for immunosuppressants.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hepatocellular carcinoma is mentioned in the brick as a cancer whose risk is increased by immunosuppression (via hepatitis B and C), not as an indication for glucocorticoids.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lung cancer is likewise cited as more common in chronically immunosuppressed patients rather than as an indication.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Melanoma is not among the malignancies the brick lists as glucocorticoid indications; the named malignancies are CLL and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Kidney cancer is described as being more common among patients receiving chronic immunosuppression, not as a glucocorticoid indication.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has taken prednisone daily for 3 years. She develops sudden midback pain after lifting a grocery bag, and imaging shows a vertebral compression fracture. Which of the following long-term effects of her therapy best accounts for this event?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone loss with osteoporosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Central fat deposition

choices.label: C
choices.text: Growth suppression

choices.label: D
choices.text: Impaired wound healing

choices.label: E
choices.text: Peripheral muscle wasting

explanation.summary: Long-term glucocorticoid use causes bone loss, leading to osteoporosis and fractures.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists bone loss among the classic features of glucocorticoid-induced hypercortisolism and, in its illustration of the long-term effects of steroids, specifically names osteoporosis, fractures, and osteonecrosis. A low-energy vertebral compression fracture after years of prednisone reflects this bone loss.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Central obesity and fat deposition (moon face, buffalo hump) alter body habitus but do not weaken vertebral bone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Growth suppression is a long-term steroid effect relevant to children, not to a 62-year-old woman with a fracture.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Impaired wound healing is a consequence of steroid immunosuppression and does not explain a fracture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Peripheral muscle wasting is a real long-term steroid effect but produces weakness and thin limbs, not a compression fracture.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with no history of diabetes has been on high-dose prednisone for 6 months for an autoimmune disease. Routine labs now show a fasting glucose of 168 mg/dL. Which of the following best explains this new finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hyperglycemia as a long-term effect of glucocorticoids

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inhibition of purine synthesis in islet cells by azathioprine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nephrotoxicity from calcineurin inhibition by tacrolimus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pancreatic damage from a cytostatic agent such as cyclophosphamide

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced IL-2 signaling in pancreatic tissue from an mTOR inhibitor

explanation.summary: Diabetes and hyperglycemia are among the long-term effects of glucocorticoid therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's overview of the long-term effects of steroids (Cushing syndrome) includes diabetes/hyperglycemia, and it lists metabolic syndrome among the classic features of glucocorticoid-induced hypercortisolism. New hyperglycemia in a patient on months of high-dose prednisone is a predictable consequence of the drug.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Purine synthesis inhibition is the mechanism of azathioprine and mycophenolate, which this patient is not taking.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity would present as a rising creatinine, and the patient is not taking a calcineurin inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The patient is taking a glucocorticoid, not a cytostatic agent, and the brick does not describe pancreatic damage as a cytostatic toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reduced IL-2 effects describe the immunophilin-binding agents and have no relationship to glucose regulation.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with a chronic autoimmune disease has required daily oral glucocorticoids for 2 years. At a well-child visit, his height has fallen from the 50th to the 10th percentile, and his arms and legs appear thin relative to his trunk. Which of the following best explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Artificial leukocytosis from reduced WBC margination

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bladder toxicity from an alkylating cytostatic agent

choices.label: C
choices.text: Growth suppression and muscle wasting from long-term steroids

choices.label: D
choices.text: Myelosuppression from damage to rapidly dividing cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced T-cell proliferation from decreased IL-2 levels

explanation.summary: Long-term glucocorticoid use suppresses growth and causes muscle wasting, producing thin arms and legs relative to the rest of the body.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's illustration of the long-term effects of steroids lists growth suppression and muscle wasting, with thin arms and legs relative to the rest of the body. Peripheral muscle wasting is also named among the classic features of glucocorticoid-induced hypercortisolism. A falling height percentile with thin extremities in a child on chronic steroids fits this pattern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Demargination leukocytosis is a laboratory effect of glucocorticoids and does not affect growth or body habitus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bladder toxicity is a cyclophosphamide effect presenting with hematuria, not with growth failure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Myelosuppression is a cytostatic-agent effect that lowers blood counts; it does not stunt growth or thin the limbs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Decreased IL-2 describes calcineurin inhibitors, which the child is not taking, and does not explain growth suppression.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman on long-term prednisone for an autoimmune disease reports gradually worsening blurred vision. Examination reveals lens opacities and elevated intraocular pressure. Which of the following best characterizes these ocular findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cataracts and glaucoma from long-term glucocorticoid use

choices.label: B
choices.text: Infiltration by Epstein-Barr virus-associated lymphoma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ocular toxicity from methotrexate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Opportunistic viral retinitis from immunosuppression

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vascular changes from calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity

explanation.summary: Glaucoma and cataracts are among the long-term effects of glucocorticoid therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's summary of the long-term effects of steroids lists glaucoma and cataracts as ocular complications. Lens opacities (cataracts) and elevated intraocular pressure (glaucoma) in a patient on chronic prednisone reflect this well-described toxicity.

whyWrongByChoice.B: EBV-linked non-Hodgkin lymphoma is a cancer risk of immunosuppression, but lens opacities with elevated eye pressure are not features of lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The patient is not taking methotrexate, and the brick attributes methotrexate toxicity to the liver, lungs, and bone marrow, not the eye.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Although immunosuppression raises infection risk, the findings of lens opacities and raised intraocular pressure are structural steroid effects, not a retinal infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity affects the kidney; the patient is on prednisone, not a calcineurin inhibitor.

questions.stem: A pharmacology student is reviewing methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, azathioprine, and mycophenolate. Although each drug acts on a different target, all four are grouped as cytostatic agents. Which of the following is the shared general mechanism that defines this class?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding to intracellular immunophilins such as FKBP

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blockade of the cellular response to IL-2 in T lymphocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibition of DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibition of the transcription factor NF-kB in immune cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mimicry of endogenous adrenal corticosteroids such as cortisol

explanation.summary: Cytostatic agents target cell growth and proliferation by inhibiting DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing immune cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines cytostatic (cyto = cell, statis = stopping) agents as drugs that target cell growth and proliferation, specifically aimed at rapidly dividing immune cells that cause damage. It states that the general mechanism of these agents, summarized in Figure 2, involves the inhibition of DNA synthesis, and the summary reiterates that cytostatic agents inhibit DNA replication, decreasing WBC proliferation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Binding to immunophilins defines the immunophilin-binding agents (tacrolimus, cyclosporine, sirolimus), not the cytostatic class.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking the response to IL-2 is the mechanism of the mTOR inhibitor sirolimus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibition of NF-kB is the mechanism of glucocorticoids.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mimicking adrenal corticosteroids describes glucocorticoids such as prednisone and dexamethasone.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with severe psoriasis is started on methotrexate. The drug reduces the availability of nucleotides needed for DNA synthesis. A deficiency of which of the following nucleotides is specifically named as the basis for methotrexate's interference with DNA synthesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adenosine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytidine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Guanosine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inosine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thymidine

explanation.summary: Methotrexate interferes with DNA synthesis by reducing nucleotide levels, specifically thymidine.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that methotrexate, a folic acid analog, competitively inhibits DHFR, an enzyme crucial for nucleic acid production, and that by reducing levels of nucleotides, specifically thymidine, it interferes with DNA synthesis. Figure 2 shows DHFR feeding both purine and pyrimidine synthesis, and thymidine is the pyrimidine nucleotide the brick singles out. Psoriasis is one of methotrexate's listed indications.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adenosine is a purine nucleotide; the brick specifically identifies thymidine as the nucleotide whose reduction underlies methotrexate's effect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytidine is a pyrimidine but is not the nucleotide the brick names for methotrexate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Guanosine is a purine; purine nucleotide depletion is more characteristic of azathioprine and mycophenolate in the brick's scheme.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inosine monophosphate is the substrate of IMP dehydrogenase, the target of mycophenolate, not the nucleotide specified for methotrexate.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman is diagnosed with an unruptured ectopic pregnancy and is hemodynamically stable. Her physician recommends medical management with a single immunosuppressive agent. Which of the following drugs is indicated for this condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Azathioprine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cyclophosphamide

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cyclosporine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Methotrexate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mycophenolate

explanation.summary: Ectopic pregnancy is among the listed indications for methotrexate.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists methotrexate's indications as RA, psoriasis, IBD, multiple types of cancer, and ectopic pregnancies. Because methotrexate targets rapidly dividing cells by interfering with DNA synthesis, it can be used to treat an ectopic pregnancy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Azathioprine is used in SLE, RA, Crohn disease, and kidney transplant rejection prevention.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cyclophosphamide is used primarily in patients with neoplasms, including solid tumors, leukemias, and lymphomas, not ectopic pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cyclosporine is used to prevent transplant rejection and in severe RA and severe psoriasis, not for ectopic pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mycophenolate is used in organ transplantation and some autoimmune diseases.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis takes prednisone, methotrexate, and folic acid. At follow-up she has elevated serum transaminases and a new dry cough with exertional dyspnea. Which of the following medications is most likely responsible for both findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Folic acid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Methotrexate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prednisone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sirolimus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tacrolimus

explanation.summary: Methotrexate damages rapidly dividing cells in the liver and lungs in addition to the bone marrow.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation on cytostatic agents notes that these drugs damage other rapidly dividing cells, including those in the liver and lungs in the case of methotrexate, and the bladder in the case of cyclophosphamide. Elevated liver enzymes together with new respiratory symptoms in a patient on methotrexate point to this drug.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Folic acid is not an immunosuppressant and is not described as causing organ toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prednisone's adverse effects described in the brick are those of hypercortisolism (Cushing syndrome), demargination leukocytosis, and immunosuppression, not liver and lung toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The patient is not taking sirolimus, and the brick does not associate the mTOR inhibitor with liver and lung damage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The patient is not taking tacrolimus, and its hallmark toxicity is nephrotoxicity, not hepatic or pulmonary injury.

questions.stem: A researcher cultures lymphoma cells in a medium supplemented with abundant purine and pyrimidine nucleotides, so that nucleotide availability is no longer rate-limiting for DNA replication. Which of the following cytostatic agents would still be expected to impair DNA replication in these cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 6-Mercaptopurine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Azathioprine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cyclophosphamide

choices.label: D
choices.text: Methotrexate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mycophenolate

explanation.summary: Cyclophosphamide cross-links DNA and blocks replication directly, independent of nucleotide supply.
explanation.whyCorrect: In Figure 2 and Table 1, cyclophosphamide acts directly at the DNA replication step by cross-linking DNA, whereas methotrexate, azathioprine (via 6-MP), and mycophenolate all act upstream by reducing the nucleotides available for de novo purine and pyrimidine synthesis. Supplying nucleotides bypasses the upstream blocks but cannot undo cross-linked DNA, so cyclophosphamide would still interfere with replication.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 6-Mercaptopurine is the active metabolite of azathioprine and likewise acts on purine nucleotide synthesis rather than on the DNA template itself.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Azathioprine works through 6-MP to block PRPP amidotransferase and purine nucleotide synthesis, which supplemental nucleotides bypass.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methotrexate inhibits DHFR to lower nucleotide (especially thymidine) levels; supplying nucleotides circumvents this block.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mycophenolate reversibly inhibits IMP dehydrogenase in purine synthesis; its effect is overcome when purine nucleotides are supplied.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with Crohn disease is maintained on azathioprine. Which of the following best describes how its active metabolite disrupts nucleic acid production?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It blocks PRPP amidotransferase by mimicking nucleotides used to make DNA and RNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: It competitively inhibits DHFR as a folic acid analog, depleting reduced folate cofactors

choices.label: C
choices.text: It cross-links DNA strands to prevent replication and transcription

choices.label: D
choices.text: It inhibits NF-kB to reduce transcription of inflammatory cytokine genes

choices.label: E
choices.text: It reversibly inhibits IMP dehydrogenase to reduce de novo purine synthesis

explanation.summary: Azathioprine's metabolite 6-MP blocks PRPP amidotransferase by mimicking the nucleotides normally used to make DNA and RNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that once absorbed, azathioprine is converted to 6-MP in tissues, disrupting purine nucleotide synthesis by blocking PRPP amidotransferase, and that it mimics nucleotides normally used to make DNA and RNA. Table 1 accordingly summarizes azathioprine as a pro-drug of 6-MP that inhibits DNA and RNA synthesis. Crohn disease is one of its listed indications.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Competitive inhibition of DHFR by a folic acid analog describes methotrexate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cross-linking DNA is the mechanism of cyclophosphamide.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibition of NF-kB is the mechanism of glucocorticoids, not azathioprine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reversible inhibition of IMP dehydrogenase is the mechanism of mycophenolate, a different purine synthesis inhibitor.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man who received a kidney transplant 8 months ago is maintained on mycophenolate. A routine complete blood count shows low hemoglobin, low white blood cell count, and low platelet count. Which of the following best explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Apoptosis of T cells from decreased cytokine production by glucocorticoids

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blocked cellular response to IL-2 in lymphocytes caused by sirolimus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibition of DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing bone marrow cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nephrotoxicity causing decreased erythropoietin production by the kidney

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced margination of leukocytes into vessel walls from steroid therapy

explanation.summary: Cytostatic agents preferentially target rapidly dividing cells, so they cause myelosuppression and resultant pancytopenia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation states that because cytostatic agents preferentially target rapidly dividing cells, potential side effects include myelosuppression and resultant pancytopenia. Mycophenolate reduces purine synthesis and DNA replication, and bone marrow cells are rapidly dividing, so all three cell lines fall.

whyWrongByChoice.A: T-cell apoptosis from decreased cytokine production is a glucocorticoid effect confined to lymphocytes; it does not lower hemoglobin and platelets.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking the response to IL-2 is the mechanism of sirolimus and affects lymphocyte proliferation, not all marrow lineages.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nephrotoxicity is characteristic of calcineurin inhibitors, and the brick does not link the patient's drug to kidney injury; a renal mechanism also would not explain low WBCs and platelets.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reduced margination is a glucocorticoid effect that raises the WBC count rather than lowering all three cell lines.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman newly diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis is prescribed methotrexate. She is puzzled because her brother takes the same drug for Crohn disease, a condition affecting the gut rather than the joints. Which of the following is the physician's best explanation for why one drug treats both diseases?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both diseases are cancers of white blood cells, and the drug cross-links their DNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both diseases are caused by the same infectious organism, and the drug eliminates it

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both diseases arise from a heightened immune response, and the drug limits production of the damaging cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both diseases represent rejection of transplanted tissue, and the drug prevents rejection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Both diseases result from folic acid deficiency, and the drug replaces the missing folate

explanation.summary: RA and Crohn disease share a heightened immune response causing inflammation and damage, and methotrexate reduces the responsible cells by inhibiting an enzyme required for their production.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the brick's case connection, the physician explains that although RA and Crohn are entirely different diseases, they share a similar mechanism: both are caused by a heightened immune response that results in inflammation and damage, to the joints in RA and to the gut in Crohn disease. Methotrexate reduces the levels of these damaging cells by inhibiting an important enzyme (DHFR) required for their production.

whyWrongByChoice.A: RA and Crohn disease are autoimmune diseases, not WBC cancers, and cross-linking DNA is the mechanism of cyclophosphamide, not methotrexate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neither disease is attributed to an infectious organism, and methotrexate is not an antimicrobial; it interferes with DNA synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neither patient has received a transplant; both have autoimmune diseases.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Methotrexate is a folic acid analog that inhibits DHFR; it antagonizes folate metabolism rather than replacing folate.

questions.stem: T cells from a patient taking cyclosporine are stimulated through the T-cell receptor in vitro. Compared with untreated T cells, which of the following is most likely to be observed in the treated cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: IL-2 is transcribed, but the IL-2 receptor fails to signal to mTOR

choices.label: B
choices.text: NF-kB is prevented from activating inflammatory cytokine genes

choices.label: C
choices.text: NFAT is dephosphorylated but cannot bind the IL-2 gene

choices.label: D
choices.text: NFAT remains phosphorylated and does not migrate into the nucleus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Signaling through CD3 and CD4 is blocked at the cell surface

explanation.summary: Calcineurin inhibitors prevent dephosphorylation of NFAT, so NFAT cannot enter the nucleus to activate IL-2 transcription.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that on TCR engagement and CD3/CD4 signaling, calcineurin dephosphorylates NFAT, enabling this transcription factor to migrate into the nucleus and activate transcription of IL-2. Cyclosporine binds cyclophilin, and the complex inhibits calcineurin, so NFAT stays phosphorylated in the cytoplasm (NFAT-P in Figure 3), IL-2 levels fall, and T-cell proliferation is reduced.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Intact IL-2 production with a blocked receptor response describes sirolimus, which inhibits mTOR, not cyclosporine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Inhibition of NF-kB is the mechanism of glucocorticoids, not calcineurin inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Calcineurin inhibition blocks the dephosphorylation step itself, so NFAT is never dephosphorylated; the defect is upstream of DNA binding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cyclosporine acts intracellularly on calcineurin downstream of TCR/CD3/CD4 signaling; it does not block the receptor complex at the surface.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl has atopic dermatitis on her face and neck that has not responded to emollients. Her dermatologist prescribes a topical calcineurin inhibitor. Which of the following drugs is she most likely prescribed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Azathioprine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Methotrexate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mycophenolate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sirolimus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tacrolimus

explanation.summary: Topical tacrolimus is used in atopic dermatitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's indications for calcineurin inhibitors include transplant rejection prevention, cyclosporine for severe active RA and severe psoriasis, and topical tacrolimus for atopic dermatitis. Tacrolimus is also indicated for prophylaxis of solid-organ (liver, heart, kidney) allograft rejection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Azathioprine is a cytostatic pro-drug of 6-MP used in SLE, RA, Crohn disease, and kidney transplantation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Methotrexate is a cytostatic agent used for RA, psoriasis, IBD, cancers, and ectopic pregnancy; it does not inhibit calcineurin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mycophenolate is a cytostatic agent used in organ transplantation and some autoimmune diseases, not a topical calcineurin inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sirolimus is the mTOR inhibitor, not a calcineurin inhibitor, and the brick lists only transplant rejection prevention as its indication.

questions.stem: A 51-year-old man has severe, active rheumatoid arthritis that has not responded to an adequate trial of methotrexate. His rheumatologist decides to add an immunophilin-binding agent that is also used in severe psoriasis. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cyclophosphamide

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cyclosporine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dexamethasone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mycophenolate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sirolimus

explanation.summary: Cyclosporine is used in severe, active RA unresponsive to methotrexate and in severe psoriasis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that, beyond preventing transplant rejection, cyclosporine is also used in severe, active RA that is unresponsive to methotrexate and in severe psoriasis. It is a calcineurin inhibitor that binds cyclophilin, placing it in the immunophilin-binding class.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cyclophosphamide is a cytostatic agent used primarily in neoplasms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dexamethasone is a glucocorticoid, not an immunophilin-binding agent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mycophenolate is a cytostatic agent, not an immunophilin-binding agent, and is used in transplantation and some autoimmune diseases.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sirolimus is an immunophilin-binding agent, but the brick lists its indication only as preventing rejection in transplant patients.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old kidney transplant recipient is maintained on sirolimus. The molecular target of this drug is best characterized as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A kinase downstream of the IL-2 receptor that regulates cell survival and proliferation

choices.label: B
choices.text: A transcription factor that drives inflammatory cytokine gene expression in the nucleus

choices.label: C
choices.text: An enzyme in purine synthesis that generates purine nucleotides for DNA replication

choices.label: D
choices.text: An enzyme that dephosphorylates NFAT after T-cell receptor engagement in the cytoplasm

choices.label: E
choices.text: An intracellular immunophilin that regulates immune responses after binding drug

explanation.summary: mTOR is a kinase downstream of IL-2 receptor signaling that regulates cell survival and proliferation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes mTOR (mammalian target of rapamycin) as a kinase crucial for regulating various cellular processes including cell survival and proliferation. Figure 4 shows the IL-2 receptor signaling through mTOR to proliferation genes; sirolimus bound to FKBP inhibits mTOR, blocking T-cell proliferation by hindering the response to IL-2.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The transcription factor driving inflammatory cytokine genes is NF-kB, the target of glucocorticoids.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Enzymes of purine synthesis (IMP dehydrogenase, PRPP amidotransferase) are targets of mycophenolate and azathioprine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The enzyme that dephosphorylates NFAT is calcineurin, the target of tacrolimus and cyclosporine, not sirolimus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: FKBP is the immunophilin that sirolimus binds, but the drug-immunophilin complex then inhibits mTOR; the immunophilin is the binding partner, not the inhibited target.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man who has taken immunosuppressants since a heart transplant 9 years ago presents with painless lymphadenopathy, night sweats, and weight loss. Biopsy confirms non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Infection with which of the following viruses is most closely linked to this malignancy in immunosuppressed patients?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytomegalovirus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Epstein-Barr virus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hepatitis B virus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hepatitis C virus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Human papillomavirus

explanation.summary: Immunosuppression heightens susceptibility to infection-associated cancers, such as Epstein-Barr virus-linked non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that because immunosuppressants suppress the immune response, they heighten susceptibility to cancers associated with infections, naming Epstein-Barr virus, which is linked to non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and the hepatitis B and C viruses, which are linked to hepatocellular carcinoma. Lymphoma in a long-term transplant recipient reflects the EBV association.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytomegalovirus is an opportunistic infection risk but is not the virus the brick links to non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepatitis B virus is linked in the brick to hepatocellular carcinoma, not lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hepatitis C virus is likewise associated with hepatocellular carcinoma in immunosuppressed patients.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Human papillomavirus is not among the infection-associated cancer links the brick describes for immunosuppression.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman on chronic immunosuppression after a liver transplant is found to have a new kidney cancer. Her son asks why immunosuppressants would increase the risk of cancer. Which of the following is the best explanation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All immunosuppressants cross-link DNA and directly cause mutations

choices.label: B
choices.text: Immunosuppressants cause demargination of WBCs that seed tumors in organs

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immunosuppressants increase cytokine production, which stimulates tumor growth

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immunosuppressants induce hypercortisolism, which transforms normal cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: One role of the immune system is to survey the body and destroy neoplastic cells

explanation.summary: Immunosuppressants raise cancer risk because the immune system normally surveys the body and destroys neoplastic cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that certain immunosuppressants carry an increased cancer risk, which makes sense given that one of the roles of the immune system is to survey the body and destroy neoplastic cells. It specifically notes that lung and kidney cancers are more common among patients receiving chronic immunosuppression, and the summary lists certain cancers alongside infections as general risks of immunosuppressive therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Only cyclophosphamide cross-links DNA; glucocorticoids and immunophilin-binding agents do not, yet chronic immunosuppression with any class raises cancer risk through loss of surveillance.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Demargination is a glucocorticoid effect that raises the circulating neutrophil count; it has nothing to do with seeding tumors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immunosuppressants decrease cytokine production (for example, glucocorticoids reduce cytokines and calcineurin inhibitors reduce IL-2); they do not increase it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hypercortisolism is a glucocorticoid-specific adverse effect, and the brick does not describe it as transforming cells into cancer.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with moderate ulcerative colitis is scheduled to begin infliximab. Before the first infusion, her physician orders a tuberculin skin test and hepatitis B serologies. Which of the following best explains why this screening is performed before starting this biologic agent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: By blocking TNF-alpha, the drug can allow reactivation of latent tuberculosis or hepatitis B

choices.label: B
choices.text: Infliximab directly damages hepatocytes, causing acute viral hepatitis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Infliximab is nephrotoxic and requires baseline assessment of renal clearance

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patients with prior tuberculosis cannot mount antibodies against the chimeric portion of the drug

choices.label: E
choices.text: The drug cross-reacts with the tuberculin antigen, invalidating future skin tests

explanation.summary: Anti-TNF biologics suppress immune surveillance of dormant pathogens, so latent TB and hepatitis B must be excluded before starting.
explanation.whyCorrect: Infliximab neutralizes TNF-alpha, a cytokine essential for maintaining granulomas and controlling intracellular pathogens. Blocking it can reactivate latent tuberculosis and hepatitis B, so the brick specifies screening with a tuberculin skin test and hepatitis serologies before initiation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Infliximab does not itself cause viral hepatitis; the concern is reactivation of pre-existing latent hepatitis B by immunosuppression.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nephrotoxicity is characteristic of calcineurin inhibitors, not anti-TNF monoclonal antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Screening is done to detect latent infection, not because prior TB affects anti-drug antibody formation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Infliximab targets TNF-alpha, not the tuberculin antigen, and does not invalidate skin testing.

questions.stem: A pharmacology student is reviewing monoclonal antibody nomenclature. She notes that a drug's generic name ends in the syllables '-ximab.' Based on the naming convention, which of the following is true of this antibody?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a chimeric antibody composed of roughly one-third murine protein

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a receptor fusion protein rather than an antibody

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is entirely murine and carries the highest risk of immunogenicity

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is fully human and contains no murine protein

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is humanized, with only the hypervariable regions derived from mouse

explanation.summary: The '-ximab' stem denotes a chimeric monoclonal antibody, which fuses murine variable regions to a human constant region and is about 33% murine.
explanation.whyCorrect: In mAb nomenclature, chimeric antibodies end in '-ximab' (e.g., cetuximab, infliximab). They combine mouse variable regions with a human immunoglobulin framework, leaving roughly one-third murine content and intermediate immunogenicity.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Fusion proteins (e.g., etanercept) do not follow the '-mab' convention at all.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fully murine antibodies end in '-omab' and are ~100% murine; '-ximab' is chimeric.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fully human antibodies end in '-umab' (e.g., nivolumab) and contain 0% murine protein.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Humanized antibodies end in '-zumab' and are only ~10% murine.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with moderate-to-severe allergic asthma and elevated serum IgE remains symptomatic despite inhaled corticosteroids. Her physician adds omalizumab. Which of the following describes this drug's mechanism of action?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It acts as a decoy receptor for IL-6

choices.label: B
choices.text: It binds free IgE

choices.label: C
choices.text: It competitively blocks the IL-1 receptor

choices.label: D
choices.text: It depletes CD20-positive B cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: It neutralizes TNF-alpha to reduce airway inflammation

explanation.summary: Omalizumab is an anti-IgE monoclonal antibody that prevents IgE from binding mast cells, blunting allergic responses.
explanation.whyCorrect: Omalizumab targets IgE, preventing it from binding to its receptor on mast cells. This is why it is indicated for allergic asthma, chronic idiopathic urticaria, and IgE-mediated food allergy/chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IL-6 pathway blockade describes tocilizumab (anti-IL-6R).
whyWrongByChoice.C: Competitive IL-1 receptor blockade describes anakinra.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CD20-directed B-cell depletion describes rituximab.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TNF-alpha neutralization describes infliximab/etanercept, not omalizumab.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis is started on etanercept. His physician explains that, unlike infliximab, etanercept is not a monoclonal antibody. Which of the following best describes the molecular structure of etanercept?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A chimeric mouse-human antibody directed against the IL-6 receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: A fully human monoclonal antibody directed against soluble TNF-alpha

choices.label: C
choices.text: A recombinant form of the IL-1 receptor antagonist that blocks IL-1 signaling

choices.label: D
choices.text: The extracellular domain of CTLA-4 fused to the Fc portion of IgG1

choices.label: E
choices.text: The extracellular domain of the TNF receptor fused to the Fc portion of IgG1

explanation.summary: Etanercept is a receptor fusion protein: a TNF-receptor extracellular domain joined to an IgG1 Fc region that acts as a soluble decoy for TNF.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fusion proteins ('-cept' agents) join a receptor's extracellular domain to an IgG Fc region. Etanercept uses the TNF receptor's extracellular domain to bind soluble TNF-alpha and TNF-beta with high affinity, acting as a decoy that keeps TNF from reaching cell-surface receptors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An anti-IL-6R agent describes tocilizumab, which is also an antibody, not a fusion protein.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Etanercept is a fusion protein, not a monoclonal antibody; anti-TNF mAbs include infliximab and adalimumab.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The recombinant IL-1 receptor antagonist is anakinra.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A CTLA-4-Fc fusion describes abatacept, not etanercept.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis inadequately controlled on methotrexate is started on abatacept. This agent is a CTLA-4-Ig fusion protein. Which of the following best explains how abatacept suppresses the immune response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds B7 and blocks CD28 costimulation of T cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: It binds soluble TNF-alpha and prevents receptor engagement

choices.label: C
choices.text: It cross-links CD3 to trigger T-cell apoptosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: It neutralizes circulating IL-1 beta

choices.label: E
choices.text: It prevents IgE from binding mast cells

explanation.summary: Abatacept is CTLA-4 fused to IgG Fc; it binds B7 (CD80/CD86) on APCs and denies T cells the CD28 costimulatory 'second signal.'
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states abatacept competitively binds B7 (CD80/CD86) on antigen-presenting cells, preventing their interaction with CD28 on T cells. Without this second signal, T cells cannot proliferate or differentiate, so the immune response is dampened.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Binding soluble TNF-alpha describes etanercept/infliximab.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Abatacept works through costimulation blockade, not CD3 cross-linking.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-1 beta is neutralized by canakinumab; IL-1 receptor blockade is anakinra.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Blocking IgE-mast cell binding describes omalizumab.

questions.stem: A neonate with a systemic inflammatory disorder involving the central nervous system is treated with anakinra, in part because this agent can penetrate the blood-brain barrier. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of anakinra?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fusion protein that acts as a decoy for IL-6

choices.label: B
choices.text: Humanized antibody against the IL-6 receptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monoclonal antibody against IL-1 beta

choices.label: D
choices.text: Monoclonal antibody against IL-17A

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recombinant IL-1 receptor antagonist

explanation.summary: Anakinra is a recombinant form of the human IL-1 receptor antagonist that competitively blocks the IL-1 receptor and can cross the blood-brain barrier.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes anakinra as a recombinant IL-1 receptor antagonist that competitively binds the IL-1 receptor, decreasing downstream inflammation. Its ability to cross the blood-brain barrier makes it useful in neonatal-onset multisystem inflammatory disease involving the brain and spinal cord.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anakinra targets the IL-1 pathway, not IL-6, and is not a decoy fusion protein.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An anti-IL-6R antibody is tocilizumab.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An antibody against IL-1 beta describes canakinumab; anakinra is a receptor antagonist protein.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An anti-IL-17A antibody is secukinumab.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with giant cell arteritis requires a steroid-sparing agent. Her rheumatologist selects tocilizumab. Against which of the following molecular targets is this humanized monoclonal antibody directed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: IgE

choices.label: B
choices.text: IL-1 beta

choices.label: C
choices.text: IL-17A

choices.label: D
choices.text: IL-6 receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: TNF-alpha

explanation.summary: Tocilizumab is a humanized anti-IL-6-receptor antibody used in giant cell arteritis, RA, and cytokine release syndrome.

explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states secukinumab is a monoclonal antibody that prevents IL-17A from binding to its receptor, and that it is effective in treating psoriasis, ankylosing spondylitis, and psoriatic arthritis.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has been receiving an anti-TNF biologic for 8 months. She now develops a malar rash, arthralgias, and a newly positive antinuclear antibody titer. Which of the following adverse effects of biologic therapy does this presentation most likely represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A demyelinating syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anaphylactic infusion reaction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bone marrow suppression

choices.label: D
choices.text: Drug-induced lupus-like syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reactivation of latent tuberculosis

explanation.summary: Anti-TNF biologics can induce an SLE-like syndrome with new antinuclear antibodies, which is why baseline ANA is checked before therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists a drug-induced lupus-like syndrome among biologic adverse effects, particularly with anti-TNF agents, and recommends baseline ANA testing so new lupus signs can be attributed to the drug. A malar rash, arthralgias, and new positive ANA in a patient on anti-TNF therapy fit this picture.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Demyelinating syndromes cause neurologic deficits, not ANA-positive arthralgias and rash.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Infusion anaphylaxis is acute (urticaria, hypotension, bronchospasm), not a subacute ANA-positive syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bone marrow suppression presents with cytopenias, not a lupus-like rash.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reactivated TB presents with fever, cough, and pulmonary findings, not a malar rash with positive ANA.

questions.stem: A physician is preparing a patient with Crohn disease to start long-term biologic therapy. Which of the following is the most appropriate step to reduce the risk of serious infection before initiating treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Administer indicated vaccinations before starting the biologic

choices.label: B
choices.text: Begin empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics for the duration of therapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Give a live attenuated vaccine immediately after the first biologic dose

choices.label: D
choices.text: Start high-dose corticosteroids to prevent infusion reactions

choices.label: E
choices.text: Withhold all screening until an infection develops

explanation.summary: Because biologics suppress immunity, indicated vaccines (pneumococcal, influenza, HBV, HPV, zoster) should be given before therapy begins.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick emphasizes that biologics increase susceptibility to infection and that mitigation includes receiving vaccines against pneumococcal disease, hepatitis, influenza, HPV, and herpes zoster before initiating treatment, ideally while the immune system can still respond.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics are not recommended and promote resistance; vaccination and screening are the strategy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Live vaccines are generally avoided during immunosuppression and should be addressed before therapy, not given after starting it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Corticosteroids add to immunosuppression and do not address infection risk from the biologic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The brick specifically calls for screening and prevention before therapy, not waiting for infection.

questions.stem: A student asks why monoclonal antibody biologics such as infliximab are administered intravenously or subcutaneously rather than by mouth. Which of the following best explains the route of administration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibodies are too small to be absorbed across the intestinal mucosa

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antibodies require gastric acid activation that only parenteral routes provide

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oral administration would lead to inactivation of the antibody

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral antibodies are preferentially cleared by the kidneys before absorption

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Fc region prevents any absorption unless the drug is inhaled

explanation.summary: As proteins, mAbs are degraded in the GI tract, so they must be given parenterally (IV, IM, or SC).
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes a disadvantage of mAbs is that they typically cannot be given orally because oral administration inactivates them in the GI tract; therefore they require more invasive routes such as intravenous, intramuscular, or subcutaneous injection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibodies are large proteins; the problem is enzymatic/acid degradation, not being too small.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibodies are inactivated—not activated—by gastric acid and proteases.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Renal clearance of intact antibodies is minimal and is not the reason oral dosing fails.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The Fc region does not require inhalation; parenteral injection is standard.

questions.stem: Among monoclonal antibodies, which of the following classes contains the least murine protein and therefore carries the lowest immunogenicity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All classes have equal immunogenicity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chimeric antibodies (-ximab)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fully human antibodies (-umab)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Humanized antibodies (-zumab)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Murine antibodies (-omab)

explanation.summary: Immunogenicity falls as murine content decreases; fully human (-umab) antibodies contain no murine protein and are least antigenic.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that murine content drives immunogenicity: murine (100%) > chimeric (~33%) > humanized (~10%) > human (0%). Fully human antibodies, ending in '-umab' (e.g., nivolumab), are the least antigenic.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Immunogenicity is not equal; it tracks directly with murine content.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chimeric antibodies are ~33% murine, more immunogenic than human ones.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Humanized antibodies still contain ~10% murine protein in their hypervariable regions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Murine antibodies are ~100% mouse-derived and are the most immunogenic.

questions.stem: A hospital pharmacy committee is comparing a new monoclonal antibody with a conventional small-molecule immunosuppressant. Which of the following features distinguishes the monoclonal antibody as a biologic agent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It acts only on the innate immune system and spares lymphocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is administered exclusively by the oral route and absorbed intact

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is derived from living culture systems or blood rather than chemical synthesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is manufactured by chemical synthesis from small organic precursors

choices.label: E
choices.text: It lacks specificity for any single molecular target or cell type

explanation.summary: Biologic agents are substances derived from living culture systems or blood, in contrast to conventional drugs made by chemical synthesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines biologic agents (biologic drugs, biologics) as substances derived from living culture systems or blood that are used to prevent, diagnose, or treat disease. They may be harvested from a natural source or produced by biotechnologic methods, which contrasts with conventional medications produced by chemical synthesis in a laboratory.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Biologics such as interleukins, antibodies, and vaccines act on many parts of the immune system, not only the innate arm.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Monoclonal antibodies typically cannot be given orally because they are inactivated in the GI tract.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chemical synthesis in a laboratory is how conventional medications are produced, not biologics.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A major advantage of biologics is their ability to target specific mechanisms; genetic engineering improved their specificity.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man received a monoclonal antibody during a clinical trial decades ago and developed a severe allergic reaction after the second dose. Review of the protocol shows the antibody's generic name ended in '-omab.' Which of the following best explains his reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The antibody contained only murine hypervariable regions on a human framework, a humanized design

choices.label: B
choices.text: The antibody depleted his B cells, and the resulting hypersensitivity reaction followed the second dose

choices.label: C
choices.text: The antibody was a receptor fusion protein with a prolonged half-life due to its Fc region

choices.label: D
choices.text: The antibody was entirely mouse-derived, and his immune system recognized the mouse protein as foreign

choices.label: E
choices.text: The antibody was fully human and cross-reacted with his own immunoglobulin light chains

explanation.summary: Murine (-omab) monoclonal antibodies are derived entirely from mice; the body recognizes the mouse component as foreign, so allergic reactions are common and many are no longer used.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that murine mAbs are derived from mice and that many are no longer in use because allergic reaction is a common side effect. The body recognizes the mouse component as foreign. Their names end in -omab, matching this patient's drug.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Only murine hypervariable regions on a human framework describes a humanized (-zumab) antibody, which is much less immunogenic.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The -omab suffix indicates murine origin, not a B-cell-depleting target; the reaction reflects foreign mouse protein.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Receptor fusion proteins are named with -cept, not -omab, and are not monoclonal antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fully human antibodies end in -umab and are the least antigenic type because their proteins are the same as in humans.

questions.stem: A drug developer is designing a monoclonal antibody in which only the murine hypervariable regions of the light and heavy chains are grafted onto a human immunoglobulin framework. Which of the following best describes the resulting antibody?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chimeric antibody, approximately 65% human protein, name ending in -ximab

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fusion protein, human Fc region joined to a receptor, name ending in -cept

choices.label: C
choices.text: Human antibody, 100% human protein, name ending in -umab

choices.label: D
choices.text: Humanized antibody, approximately 95% human protein, name ending in -zumab

choices.label: E
choices.text: Murine antibody, 0% human protein, name ending in -omab

explanation.summary: Humanized mAbs graft only the murine hypervariable regions onto a human framework, leaving about 95% human protein, and are named with -zumab.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes humanized mAbs as derived from fusing the murine hypervariable regions on the light and heavy chains to a human immunoglobulin framework. The final immunoglobulin is about 95% human protein (about 10% murine in figure 1), giving less immunogenicity than chimeric antibodies. Their names end in -zumab, as in trastuzumab.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chimeric antibodies fuse human constant regions to entire murine variable regions (not just hypervariable regions) and are about 65% human.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fusion proteins are receptor extracellular domains joined to IgG Fc, not antibodies with grafted hypervariable regions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Human antibodies contain no murine protein at all; they are produced from cells carrying the human immunoglobulin gene.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Murine antibodies are entirely mouse-derived and would not have a human framework.

questions.stem: A biotechnology company produces a monoclonal antibody named nivolumab. Which of the following manufacturing approaches is used to generate this class of antibody?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Animal cells carrying an inserted human immunoglobulin gene in their genome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Attachment of a receptor extracellular domain to an IgG Fc region

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fusion of human constant regions with mouse variable regions

choices.label: D
choices.text: Grafting of murine hypervariable regions onto a human framework

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mouse hybridoma cells producing unmodified mouse immunoglobulin

explanation.summary: Fully human (-umab) mAbs are made in animal cells that have the human immunoglobulin gene inserted into their genome, yielding proteins identical to human ones.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nivolumab ends in -umab, marking it as a human mAb. The brick explains that human mAbs are derived from animal cells that have the human immunoglobulin gene inserted in their genome; because the resulting proteins are the same as in humans, they are the least antigenic type of mAb.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Attaching a receptor domain to an Fc region produces a receptor fusion protein (-cept), not an antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fusing human constant regions with mouse variable regions yields a chimeric (-ximab) antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Grafting murine hypervariable regions onto a human framework yields a humanized (-zumab) antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Unmodified mouse immunoglobulin describes murine (-omab) antibodies, which are highly immunogenic.

questions.stem: A pharmacology student is analyzing the name cetuximab. She notes it is composed of roughly two-thirds human and one-third mouse protein. Which portions of this antibody are derived from the mouse?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only the hypervariable regions within the variable domains

choices.label: B
choices.text: The constant regions of the heavy chains only

choices.label: C
choices.text: The entire immunoglobulin molecule

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Fc region and the hinge

choices.label: E
choices.text: The variable regions of the light and heavy chains

explanation.summary: Chimeric (-ximab) antibodies combine human constant regions with murine variable regions, making the whole variable region mouse-derived.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes chimeric mAbs as derived from fusing the constant regions of human immunoglobulin with the variable regions from a non-human source, usually mice; the final product is about 65% human. Figure 1 labels the murine variable regions as the mouse component of the chimerized antibody. Cetuximab is the brick's example of a -ximab.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mouse-derived hypervariable regions alone describe a humanized (-zumab) antibody, which is about 95% human.
whyWrongByChoice.B: In chimeric antibodies the constant regions are the human component, not the mouse component.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An entirely mouse-derived molecule is a murine (-omab) antibody, 100% murine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The Fc region belongs to the human constant portion of a chimeric antibody.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man with COVID-19 is treated with the combination bamlanivimab plus etesevimab. Based on the substem in these drug names, which of the following is the target class of these monoclonal antibodies?

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

explanation.whyCorrect: Table 1 of the brick lists target-based substems: v(i)/vi(r) indicates a virus, with bamlanivimab plus etesevimab (for SARS-COVID) as the example. Nomenclature can therefore be read from the name to identify the target cell, molecule, or organ.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A bone target is denoted by s(o), as in denosumab.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An interleukin target is denoted by k(i) or ki(n), as in ustekinumab.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A toxin target is denoted by tox(a), as in tosatoxumab.

explanation.summary: Trastuzumab carries the tumor substem t(u) and the humanized suffix -zumab.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick uses trastuzumab as its example of a humanized (-zumab) mAb and, in Table 1, as the example of the t(u) substem indicating a tumor target (breast cancer). Reading the name from its parts gives a humanized antibody directed at a tumor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chimeric antibodies end in -ximab; trastuzumab ends in -zumab.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Human antibodies end in -umab, and an interleukin target would use the k(i) substem.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The bone substem is s(o), as in denosumab, not t(u).
whyWrongByChoice.E: Murine antibodies end in -omab, and the toxin substem is tox(a).

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with plaque psoriasis is started on ustekinumab. Using the nomenclature system, which of the following can be inferred from the substem 'ki' in this drug's name?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.text: The antibody is of murine origin

choices.label: C
choices.text: The antibody targets a bacterial toxin

choices.label: D

explanation.summary: The substem k(i) or ki(n) indicates an interleukin target; ustekinumab is the brick's example, directed against IL-12.
explanation.whyCorrect: Table 1 lists k(i), ki(n) as the substem for an interleukin target with ustekinumab (IL-12) as the example. The -umab ending separately indicates it is a fully human antibody.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fusion proteins are named with -cept and do not use the -mab system at all.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Murine origin would be signaled by an -omab ending; ustekinumab ends in -umab (human).
whyWrongByChoice.C: A toxin target uses the tox(a) substem, as in tosatoxumab.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A viral target uses v(i) or vi(r), as in bamlanivimab.

explanation.whyCorrect: Table 1 of the brick lists tox(a) as the substem for a toxin target, with tosatoxumab (resistant Staphylococcus infections) as the example.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bone targets are indicated by s(o), as in denosumab.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Interleukin targets are indicated by k(i) or ki(n), as in ustekinumab.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tumor targets are indicated by t(u), as in trastuzumab.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman with bone cancer is treated with denosumab. Based on the nomenclature system for monoclonal antibodies, which of the following is true of this drug?

choices.text: It is a fully human antibody with a bone-related target

choices.label: D

explanation.summary: Denosumab combines the s(o) bone substem with the -umab human suffix.
explanation.whyCorrect: Table 1 lists s(o) as the substem for a bone target, with denosumab (bone cancer) as the example. The -umab ending indicates a fully human antibody, the least antigenic class.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chimeric antibodies end in -ximab, and a tumor target uses t(u); denosumab has neither.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fusion proteins end in -cept; toxin targets use tox(a).
whyWrongByChoice.D: Humanized antibodies end in -zumab, and interleukin targets use k(i).

questions.stem: A student notes that the target substem for viruses is written as 'v(i)' and the substem for bone as 's(o)', with a vowel shown in parentheses. Which of the following best explains when the parenthetical vowel is included in a monoclonal antibody's name?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only as needed for pronunciation when the following substem begins with a consonant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only when the antibody has been approved as a biosimilar to an existing product

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only when the antibody has more than one molecular target in the same pathway

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only when the antibody is intended for intravenous rather than subcutaneous administration

choices.label: E
choices.text: Only when the antibody is of humanized rather than human origin, as marked by -zumab

explanation.summary: The parenthetical vowel in a target substem is a pronunciation aid, added only if the next substem starts with a consonant.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the second letter (a vowel) in parentheses is added only as needed to make the drug name easier to pronounce if substem B starts with a consonant. It carries no information about origin, route, or target number.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Biosimilar status is unrelated to the naming substems.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The number of targets is not encoded by the optional vowel.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy with cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome (CAPS) has recurrent fevers, rash, and joint pain. His rheumatologist starts canakinumab. Which of the following is the molecular target of this drug?

choices.text: Interleukin-1 beta

choices.text: Interleukin-1 receptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Interleukin-17A

choices.label: D

choices.label: E

explanation.summary: Canakinumab is a monoclonal antibody against IL-1 beta used in autoinflammatory periodic fever syndromes such as CAPS.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that canakinumab targets IL-1 beta, reducing inflammation in autoimmune disease, with indications including cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome (CAPS), TNF receptor-associated periodic syndrome (TRAPS), mevalonate kinase deficiency (MKD), familial Mediterranean fever (FMF), and hyperimmunoglobulin D syndrome (HIDS).

whyWrongByChoice.B: The IL-1 receptor is the target of anakinra, a recombinant receptor antagonist, not of canakinumab.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-17A is the target of secukinumab.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The IL-6 receptor is the target of tocilizumab.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TNF-alpha is the target of infliximab and etanercept.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman with recurrent painful nodules and draining sinus tracts in the axillae and groin is diagnosed with hidradenitis suppurativa. After failure of antibiotics, her dermatologist prescribes a biologic that blocks IL-17A from binding its receptor. Which of the following agents was most likely prescribed?

choices.text: Abatacept

choices.label: B
choices.text: Canakinumab

choices.label: C
choices.text: Omalizumab

choices.label: D
choices.text: Secukinumab

choices.label: E

explanation.summary: Secukinumab, an anti-IL-17A monoclonal antibody, is effective in hidradenitis suppurativa as well as psoriasis and ankylosing spondylitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes secukinumab as a monoclonal antibody that binds IL-17A and prevents it from binding its receptor, with proven effectiveness in psoriasis, ankylosing spondylitis, and hidradenitis suppurativa.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Abatacept is a CTLA4-Ig fusion protein that blocks T-cell costimulation; it is not an IL-17A inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Canakinumab targets IL-1 beta and is used in periodic fever syndromes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Omalizumab targets IgE and is used for asthma, urticaria, food allergy, and nasal polyps.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tocilizumab blocks the IL-6 receptor and is used in giant cell arteritis, RA, and cytokine release syndrome.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman has had daily hives for 9 months without an identifiable trigger, and she remains symptomatic despite high-dose antihistamines. Which of the following biologics is indicated for her condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Abatacept

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anakinra

choices.label: C
choices.text: Etanercept

choices.label: D
choices.text: Omalizumab

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secukinumab

explanation.summary: Chronic idiopathic urticaria is an indication for omalizumab, which prevents IgE from binding mast cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists the indications for omalizumab as asthma, chronic idiopathic urticaria, IgE-mediated food allergy, and chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps. Months of hives without an identifiable cause is chronic idiopathic urticaria, and omalizumab keeps IgE from binding its receptors on mast cells, reducing degranulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Abatacept blocks T-cell costimulation for RA, psoriatic arthritis, JIA, and GVHD.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Anakinra blocks the IL-1 receptor and is used for RA, neonatal-onset multisystem inflammatory disease, and IL-1 receptor antagonist deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Etanercept is a TNF decoy used for ankylosing spondylitis, plaque psoriasis, JIA, PA, and RA, not urticaria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Secukinumab blocks IL-17A for psoriasis, ankylosing spondylitis, and hidradenitis suppurativa.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man develops high fever, hypotension, and hypoxia 3 days after receiving chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy for leukemia; the syndrome is attributed to massive cytokine release. Which of the following biologics is indicated to treat this condition?

explanation.summary: Tocilizumab, the humanized anti-IL-6 receptor antibody, is used to treat cytokine release syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists tocilizumab's indications as giant cell arteritis, RA, and cytokine release syndrome. It is a humanized IgG monoclonal antibody that competitively inhibits binding of IL-6 to its receptor (IL-6R), blunting the inflammatory cascade in this syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Abatacept blocks CD28 costimulation for RA, JIA, PA, and GVHD, not for cytokine release syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Etanercept is a TNF decoy used for rheumatologic and psoriatic disease; the brick does not list it for cytokine release syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Omalizumab targets IgE for allergic conditions and has no role in cytokine release syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Secukinumab blocks IL-17A for psoriasis-spectrum disease, not cytokine release syndrome.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man undergoes hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for leukemia. To reduce the risk of graft-versus-host disease, his transplant team adds a fusion protein that prevents donor T cells from receiving the CD28 costimulatory signal. Which of the following agents was most likely added?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Abatacept

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anakinra

choices.label: C
choices.text: Etanercept

choices.label: D
choices.text: Infliximab

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tocilizumab

explanation.summary: Abatacept, a CTLA4-Fc fusion protein that blocks B7-CD28 costimulation, is indicated for graft-versus-host disease in addition to RA, psoriatic arthritis, and polyarticular JIA.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes abatacept as the extracellular domain of CTLA4 fused to the Fc portion of IgG; it competitively binds B7 (CD80/CD86) on antigen-presenting cells so T cells cannot receive the CD28 signal needed for proliferation and differentiation. Its listed indications include RA, psoriatic arthritis, polyarticular JIA, and graft-versus-host disease (GVHD).

whyWrongByChoice.B: Anakinra is an IL-1 receptor antagonist, not a fusion protein, and GVHD is not among its listed indications.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Etanercept is a TNF receptor-Fc fusion that neutralizes TNF; it does not block CD28 costimulation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Infliximab is an anti-TNF-alpha monoclonal antibody used for IBD, RA, ankylosing spondylitis, and psoriasis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tocilizumab is an anti-IL-6 receptor antibody used for giant cell arteritis, RA, and cytokine release syndrome.

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical scientist explains that receptor fusion proteins such as etanercept remain in the circulation far longer than the unfused receptor would. Which of the following best explains this persistence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Fc region blocks hepatic uptake by binding complement component C1q, slowing clearance

choices.label: B
choices.text: The fusion protein is stored in mast cell granules and released slowly into the circulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: The IgG Fc region is recognized by the neonatal Fc receptor, which binds and prolongs the molecule's life

choices.label: D
choices.text: The receptor domain is glycosylated so heavily that renal filtration through the glomerulus is impossible

choices.label: E
choices.text: The receptor portion binds the target with such high affinity that the complex is never cleared from blood

explanation.summary: Fusing a receptor to the IgG Fc region lets the neonatal Fc receptor in the bloodstream bind the molecule and extend its half-life.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that receptor fusion proteins ('IgG1 fusion proteins') consist of a receptor's extracellular domain fused with the Fc region of IgG, and that the Fc region is recognized by the neonatal Fc receptor in the bloodstream, which binds and prolongs the life of the molecule. This longer half-life enhances the desirability of the drug product.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complement binding is not the mechanism described for prolonged survival of fusion proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fusion proteins are not stored in mast cell granules; mast cells are relevant to IgE and omalizumab.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick attributes the longer half-life to the Fc region and neonatal Fc receptor, not to glycosylation of the receptor domain.
whyWrongByChoice.E: High target affinity explains efficacy as a decoy, not the persistence of the molecule in blood.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is switched from infliximab to etanercept. Her rheumatologist notes that etanercept neutralizes an additional cytokine that infliximab does not bind. Which of the following is that cytokine?

choices.label: A
choices.text: IL-1 beta

choices.label: B
choices.text: IL-12

choices.label: C
choices.text: IL-17A

choices.label: D
choices.text: IL-6

choices.label: E
choices.text: TNF-beta

explanation.summary: Etanercept binds both soluble TNF-alpha and TNF-beta with high affinity, whereas infliximab is an antibody specific for TNF-alpha.
