explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that etanercept binds to soluble TNF-alpha and TNF-beta with much greater affinity than the TNF receptor, so less free TNF-alpha and TNF-beta is available to bind the receptor. Infliximab, by contrast, is described as targeting TNF-alpha only.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IL-1 beta is the target of canakinumab, and its receptor is blocked by anakinra; neither anti-TNF agent binds it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-12 is the target of ustekinumab.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-17A is the target of secukinumab.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-6 signaling is blocked by tocilizumab at the receptor, not by etanercept.

questions.stem: A drug class is described as molecules that bind either an interleukin itself or the interleukin's receptor site, thereby inhibiting interleukin signal transduction. Which of the following is the effect of this inhibition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blunting of the inflammatory response

choices.label: B
choices.text: Depletion of circulating B cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enhanced mast cell degranulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased T-cell costimulation through CD28

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prolonged survival of soluble TNF-alpha

explanation.summary: Interleukin-receptor modulators inhibit interleukin signal transduction, which blunts the inflammatory response.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines interleukin-receptor modulators as molecules that bind either the interleukin or the interleukin receptor site, and states that inhibition of interleukin signal transduction blunts the inflammatory response. Anakinra is the example given.

whyWrongByChoice.B: B-cell depletion is a separate biologic mechanism listed in the brick, not the result of interleukin receptor modulation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mast cell degranulation is reduced, not enhanced, by biologics acting on allergic pathways (omalizumab); interleukin blockade does not enhance it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CD28 costimulation is blocked by abatacept; interleukin-receptor modulators do not increase it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TNF-alpha survival is unrelated to interleukin receptor modulation; etanercept and infliximab reduce free TNF.

questions.stem: A 3-week-old infant presents with pustular rash, osteomyelitis, and marked systemic inflammation. Genetic testing reveals deficiency of the IL-1 receptor antagonist. Which of the following agents directly replaces the missing protein's function?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Abatacept

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anakinra

choices.label: C
choices.text: Canakinumab

choices.label: D
choices.text: Etanercept

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tocilizumab

explanation.summary: Anakinra is a recombinant form of the human IL-1 receptor antagonist, so it is indicated for IL-1 receptor antagonist deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes anakinra as a recombinant form of the human IL-1 receptor antagonist that competitively binds the IL-1 receptor and lists IL-1 receptor-antagonist deficiency among its indications, along with RA and neonatal-onset multisystem inflammatory disease. Because it is the recombinant antagonist itself, it directly restores the missing inhibitory function.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Abatacept blocks T-cell costimulation and has no role in IL-1 receptor antagonist deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Canakinumab neutralizes IL-1 beta with an antibody but is not the receptor antagonist protein and is listed for CAPS, TRAPS, MKD, FMF, and HIDS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Etanercept is a TNF decoy and does not act on IL-1 signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tocilizumab blocks the IL-6 receptor, not the IL-1 pathway.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis asks why her physician recommends a biologic agent over a conventional broad immunosuppressant. Which of the following is the major advantage of biologics cited for this choice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are less expensive than conventional immunosuppressant medications

choices.label: B
choices.text: They can be taken orally, improving convenience and adherence for chronic therapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: They carry no risk of reactivating latent tuberculosis or hepatitis B

choices.label: D
choices.text: They never provoke antibodies against the drug that reduce its efficacy

choices.label: E
choices.text: They target specific mechanisms, reducing indiscriminate immunosuppression

explanation.summary: Biologics act on specific molecular targets, minimizing unintended consequences and indiscriminate immunosuppression.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that a major advantage of biologics is their ability to target specific mechanisms, minimizing the risk of unintended consequences and adverse effects, and the summary notes they offer specificity while reducing indiscriminate immunosuppression. In chronic inflammatory rheumatic disease they slow progression, reduce pain and swelling, and decrease joint damage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cost is listed as a factor limiting biologic choice; biosimilars, not biologics in general, are noted as a more affordable alternative.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Monoclonal antibodies typically cannot be given orally; they require IV, IM, or SC routes, which is a disadvantage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reactivation of latent TB or hepatitis B is a recognized risk of biologics.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Generation of antibodies against the biologic agent is a listed side effect.

questions.stem: After the patent on a monoclonal antibody expires, a second manufacturer markets a product with a primary amino acid sequence matching the original. Which of the following best describes this product?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A biosimilar that underwent FDA evaluation for quality, safety, and efficacy and may be less expensive

choices.label: B
choices.text: A chemically synthesized copy produced without living cells, culture systems, or bioreactors

choices.label: C
choices.text: A fusion protein engineered to have a longer half-life than the original antibody in the circulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: A generic small molecule that can be marketed without any FDA regulatory review or clinical testing

choices.label: E
choices.text: A humanized version of the original murine antibody carrying a new variable region sequence and framework

explanation.summary: Biosimilars are nearly identical copies of biologics, with matching primary amino acid sequences, that are rigorously evaluated by the FDA and may be cheaper to manufacture.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation explains that biosimilars, nearly identical copies of biologics, become possible after patent expiration. Their primary amino acid sequences match their biologic counterparts, they undergo rigorous FDA evaluation ensuring quality, safety, and efficacy, and they may be less expensive to manufacture, offering a more affordable alternative.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Biologics and their biosimilars are derived from living systems, not chemical synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A biosimilar copies the original biologic; it is not converted into a fusion protein.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Biologics are not small molecules, and the brick emphasizes that biosimilars undergo rigorous FDA evaluation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Changing a murine antibody to a humanized one alters its structure; a biosimilar matches the original sequence.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman with Crohn disease responded well to infliximab for a year but now has recurrent symptoms. Laboratory testing shows circulating antibodies directed against the drug. Which structural feature of infliximab best explains this development?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a chimeric antibody containing murine variable regions

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a fully human antibody with no foreign protein

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a humanized antibody with only murine hypervariable regions

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a receptor fusion protein containing an IgG Fc region

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a recombinant receptor antagonist protein

explanation.summary: Generation of antibodies against the biologic is a listed side effect, and infliximab's chimeric (-ximab) structure with about one-third murine protein makes it more immunogenic than humanized or human antibodies.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists generation of antibodies against the biologic agent as a common side effect. Infliximab ends in -ximab, identifying it as a chimeric mAb that fuses human constant regions to murine variable regions; because chimeric antibodies retain about 33% murine protein, they carry more immunogenicity than humanized or human antibodies.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Fully human antibodies end in -umab and are the least antigenic; infliximab is not one.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Humanized antibodies end in -zumab and are about 95% human; infliximab is chimeric.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fusion proteins end in -cept (etanercept, abatacept); infliximab is a monoclonal antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A recombinant receptor antagonist describes anakinra, not infliximab.

questions.stem: Before starting a biologic for rheumatoid arthritis, a 58-year-old man has a complete blood count, liver function tests, and a lipid/cholesterol panel drawn. Which of the following adverse effects of some biologic agents is the lipid panel intended to detect during subsequent monitoring?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elevation of hepatic transaminases and conjugated bilirubin levels

choices.label: B
choices.text: Emergence of antinuclear and anti-dsDNA autoantibodies on testing

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increases in low-density lipoprotein and triglyceride levels

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reactivation of latent hepatitis B virus or tuberculosis infection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Suppression of bone marrow with cytopenias in all three lineages

explanation.summary: Some biologics raise LDL and triglyceride levels, so a baseline lipid/cholesterol panel is part of pre-treatment evaluation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists baseline assessments before biologic therapy, including a complete blood count, lipid/cholesterol panel, and liver function testing, and explains that this is necessary because some biologics cause liver enzyme elevation, bone marrow suppression, and/or increases in low-density lipoprotein and triglyceride levels. The lipid panel specifically addresses the last of these.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Liver enzyme elevation is monitored with liver function testing, not the lipid panel.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antinuclear antibody emergence is assessed with baseline ANA testing, particularly with anti-TNF agents.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hepatitis B reactivation is screened for with antibody panels for hepatitis B and C.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bone marrow suppression is monitored with the complete blood count.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman is bitten by a bat while camping, raising concern for rabies exposure. To provide defense that begins working immediately, before her own immune system has time to respond, her physician administers preformed antibodies against the pathogen. Which of the following best describes this intervention?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A live attenuated vaccine inducing a self-limited infection

choices.label: B
choices.text: A toxoid vaccine neutralizing a bacterial toxin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Active immunization generating durable memory cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: An mRNA vaccine instructing host cells to make antigen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passive immunization providing rapid protection

explanation.summary: Transferring preformed antibodies is passive immunization, which acts immediately but does not generate memory.
explanation.whyCorrect: Passive immunization involves transferring antibodies from another source into an individual. Because functional antibody is delivered directly, protection is immediate rather than waiting the 2-4 weeks an active response requires. However, the transferred antibodies have a half-life of only a few weeks, so protection is short-lived and no memory cells are formed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A live attenuated vaccine is a form of active immunization that must induce the patient's own response over weeks and is not preformed antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A toxoid is an active vaccine against a bacterial toxin (e.g., tetanus); it is not preformed antibody and gives no immediate protection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Active immunization stimulates the person's own immune system and takes 2-4 weeks to develop; it would not provide immediate protection after an acute exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An mRNA vaccine directs host cells to synthesize antigen and mount an active response, which is delayed, not immediate.

questions.stem: A 2-month-old infant born to a mother who is immune to measles is exposed to a sibling with measles but does not become ill. Serologic testing detects measles-specific IgG in the infant's blood, even though the infant has never been vaccinated. Which of the following best explains the infant's protection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A primary adaptive response generated by the infant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Maternal IgG transferred across the placenta

choices.label: C
choices.text: Memory B cells inherited from the mother

choices.label: D
choices.text: Monoclonal antibodies administered at birth

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secretory IgA transferred through breast milk

explanation.summary: Natural passive immunity in early infancy comes from maternal IgG that crossed the placenta using the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn).
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes natural passive immunization as including the transfer of IgG antibodies across the placenta to the developing fetus via the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn). This gives the newborn circulating maternal IgG, explaining the measles-specific serum IgG in an unvaccinated 2-month-old.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A primary response by the infant would take weeks to produce antibody and would not explain pre-existing IgG at the time of exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Memory cells are not transferred across the placenta; only antibodies (IgG) are passed to the fetus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: No monoclonal antibody product was given; the scenario describes naturally acquired protection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IgA is transferred in breast milk and acts at mucosal surfaces such as the gut; it would not account for measles-specific IgG measured in the serum.

questions.stem: A patient with a congenital antibody deficiency receives monthly intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). He is well protected against infection while receiving the infusions, but becomes susceptible again within a few weeks if therapy is stopped. Which property of this form of immunization best explains why the protection is not lasting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It drives class switching in the patient's B cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: It generates long-lived memory B cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: It provides protection that does not create memory cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: It requires 2-4 weeks before any protection begins

choices.label: E
choices.text: It stimulates the patient's own plasma cells to make antibody

explanation.summary: Passive immunization gives immediate but transient protection because it supplies antibody without generating memory.
explanation.whyCorrect: IVIG is passive immunization: it delivers pooled polyclonal antibodies but does not engage the patient's own immune system. The brick states passive immunization does not generate an immune response in the patient, so memory cells do not form and, because antibodies have a half-life of roughly 3 weeks, protection lapses when infusions stop.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Class switching occurs in the recipient's own B cells during an active response, which passive antibody transfer does not trigger.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Passive immunization does not generate memory B cells; that is a feature of active immunization.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Passive immunization actually acts immediately; the delay of 2-4 weeks is characteristic of active immunization.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Passively transferred antibody does not stimulate the patient's plasma cells; the antibody is supplied ready-made.

questions.stem: A child receives a booster dose of a vaccine several months after the initial series. Compared with the response to the first dose, the antibodies produced after the booster are both more abundant and bind the antigen more tightly. This improvement is primarily due to which of the following processes occurring in B cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Affinity maturation and class switching

choices.label: B
choices.text: Positive and negative selection of thymocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: T-independent activation of B cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transplacental transfer of maternal antibody

choices.label: E
choices.text: VDJ recombination generating the naive receptor repertoire

explanation.summary: Booster doses strengthen the response by promoting class switching and affinity maturation in B cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that subsequent doses, known as boosters, strengthen the adaptive response by promoting class switching and affinity maturation in B cells. This is why a secondary response yields greater quantity and higher-affinity (better quality) antibody than the primary response.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Thymic selection shapes the T-cell repertoire and is not the mechanism by which booster antibodies gain affinity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: T-independent responses are low-affinity and lack memory; they do not account for the enhanced, higher-affinity booster response.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Maternal antibody transfer is passive immunity and does not explain improved antibody made by the child's own B cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: VDJ recombination creates the initial naive B-cell receptor repertoire and does not improve affinity on re-exposure.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with HIV and a CD4+ count of 150 cells/mm^3 presents to update his immunizations. Which type of vaccine is contraindicated in this patient because the weakened pathogen could replicate in an uncontrolled manner?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conjugate polysaccharide

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inactivated

choices.label: C
choices.text: Live attenuated

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recombinant subunit

choices.label: E
choices.text: Toxoid

explanation.summary: Live attenuated vaccines are contraindicated in immunocompromised patients because the attenuated pathogen may replicate uncontrolled.
explanation.whyCorrect: Live attenuated vaccines contain a living, weakened pathogen. In an immunocompromised host, the brick notes this can cause severe or fatal infection, and the pathogen may revert to a virulent form. A CD4+ count below 200 cells/mm^3 indicates significant immunodeficiency, making LAVs contraindicated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Conjugate polysaccharide vaccines are non-replicating subunit vaccines and can be given safely to immunocompromised patients.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Inactivated vaccines contain killed pathogen that cannot infect or replicate, so they are safe in immunodeficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Recombinant subunit vaccines contain only an antigenic protein and pose no infection risk to immunocompromised patients.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Toxoid vaccines contain an inactivated toxin, cannot replicate, and are safe in immunocompromised patients.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman who is 12 weeks pregnant is reviewing her vaccination record with her physician. Which of the following vaccines is contraindicated during her pregnancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inactivated influenza (injected)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pneumococcal conjugate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Recombinant hepatitis B

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tetanus toxoid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Varicella (live attenuated)

explanation.summary: Live attenuated vaccines such as varicella are contraindicated in pregnancy because the virus could cross the placenta.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists pregnancy as a contraindication for live attenuated vaccines, specifically including varicella and MMR. If a pregnant person is infected with the vaccine virus, it can theoretically cross the placenta and cause congenital fetal infection and birth defects, so these live vaccines are avoided.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The injected influenza vaccine is inactivated (killed) and is recommended, not contraindicated, during pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The pneumococcal conjugate vaccine is a non-replicating subunit vaccine and poses no risk of fetal infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Recombinant hepatitis B is a non-live subunit vaccine and is not contraindicated in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tetanus toxoid contains an inactivated toxin, does not replicate, and is safely given in pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old farmer sustains a deep laceration on a fence. His physician recommends a vaccine that is directed against the toxin produced by Clostridium tetani rather than against the bacterium itself, so that the immune response can neutralize the toxin. Which type of vaccine is this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conjugate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Live attenuated

choices.label: C
choices.text: mRNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: Toxoid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Viral vector

explanation.summary: Tetanus is a toxin-mediated disease, so it is prevented with a toxoid vaccine made from an inactivated toxin.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that toxoid vaccines contain inactivated toxins and are relevant to toxin-mediated disease, where the effective immune response is antibodies directed against the toxin so that it can be neutralized. Tetanus and diphtheria are the classic examples given.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Conjugate vaccines link a capsular polysaccharide to a protein to target encapsulated bacteria, not a secreted toxin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A live attenuated vaccine uses a weakened whole pathogen, not an inactivated toxin, and is not used for toxin-mediated tetanus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An mRNA vaccine directs host cells to make a protein antigen and is not the platform described for neutralizing tetanus toxin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Viral vector vaccines deliver a pathogen gene in a carrier virus and are used against viral antigens, not bacterial toxins.

questions.stem: A vaccine against Streptococcus pneumoniae is manufactured by covalently linking the bacterial capsular polysaccharide to a carrier protein. Compared with a vaccine made of the pure polysaccharide alone, what key advantage does this conjugation provide?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It allows the vaccine to replicate within the host

choices.label: B
choices.text: It converts a T-independent antigen into a T-dependent one

choices.label: C
choices.text: It provides immediate passive protection with preformed antibody

choices.label: D
choices.text: It removes the need for any antigen in the vaccine

choices.label: E
choices.text: It transforms the preparation into a live attenuated vaccine

explanation.summary: Conjugating a polysaccharide to a protein makes it a T-dependent antigen, producing high-affinity antibody and memory.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that polysaccharides alone are T-independent antigens that generate only a low-affinity response without memory. Covalently linking (conjugating) the polysaccharide to a peptide or protein makes it a T-dependent antigen, so follicular helper T cells provide help to B cells, driving affinity maturation, memory B-cell formation, and an improved response even in young children.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Conjugate vaccines are non-replicating subunit vaccines; they do not replicate in the host.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Conjugate vaccines induce active immunity; they do not supply preformed antibody for immediate protection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The polysaccharide antigen is still required; conjugation adds a carrier protein rather than eliminating antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A conjugate vaccine is a subunit vaccine, not a live attenuated preparation.

questions.stem: A subunit vaccine contains only a purified antigen and, on its own, produces a weak memory response. Aluminum salts (alum) are added to the formulation to strengthen the response. What is the primary role of this added component?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It acts as an adjuvant

choices.label: B
choices.text: It covalently binds the antigen, converting it into a toxoid

choices.label: C
choices.text: It enables the antigen to replicate inside host cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: It neutralizes bacterial toxins at the injection site

choices.label: E
choices.text: It supplies preformed antibodies for immediate protection

explanation.summary: Adjuvants such as alum amplify the immune response by enhancing dendritic cell uptake and presentation of antigen.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines adjuvants as compounds added to vaccines to amplify the immune response. Alum, the most commonly used adjuvant, interacts with the membrane of dendritic cells and enhances the uptake and presentation of antigens. Adjuvants are especially needed for subunit vaccines that otherwise produce a weak memory response.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick explicitly states adjuvants are not covalently bound to the vaccine antigen, and alum does not create a toxoid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Adjuvants do not allow antigen to replicate; they enhance the host immune response to the antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alum does not neutralize toxins; neutralizing a toxin is the role of antibodies raised against a toxoid.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Adjuvants do not contain antibodies; supplying preformed antibody would be passive immunization, not adjuvant activity.

questions.stem: An immunocompromised patient needs protection against SARS-CoV-2. The physician selects a vaccine in which a lipid nanoparticle delivers genetic instructions that cause the patient's own cells to synthesize the viral spike protein and display it on class I and class II MHC molecules. Which type of vaccine is this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inactivated

choices.label: B
choices.text: Live attenuated

choices.label: C
choices.text: mRNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: Polysaccharide

choices.label: E
choices.text: Toxoid

explanation.summary: mRNA vaccines use a lipid nanoparticle to deliver mRNA so host cells make the antigen and present it on class I and II MHC.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes mRNA vaccines as introducing mRNA stabilized in a lipid nanoparticle (which also acts as an adjuvant); host cells then produce viral proteins presented on class I and II MHC. Because there is no live pathogen, mRNA vaccines can elicit cytotoxic T cells while being safe to give to immunocompromised people, unlike a live vaccine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Inactivated vaccines contain killed whole pathogen and generate mainly humoral immunity; they do not instruct host cells to make antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A live attenuated vaccine contains replicating pathogen and is contraindicated in immunocompromised patients; it does not work by delivering mRNA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Polysaccharide vaccines are made of capsular sugars and do not cause host cells to synthesize antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Toxoid vaccines consist of an inactivated toxin and do not deliver genetic material via a lipid nanoparticle.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl undergoing chemotherapy cannot receive live vaccines and has a weakened immune system. She nonetheless remains protected from measles because roughly 95% of her community is vaccinated, so the pathogen cannot spread easily enough to reach her. This protection is best described as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Affinity maturation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Herd immunity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Natural active immunity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passive immunity

choices.label: E
choices.text: The adjuvant effect

explanation.summary: Herd immunity protects susceptible individuals when a sufficient fraction of the population is immune.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines herd immunity as resistance to the spread of an infectious disease within a population once a sufficient percentage (70-95%, depending on infectivity) is immune. It is described as critical for protecting those who cannot receive or respond to a vaccine, such as immunocompromised patients, because an infected person is unlikely to encounter a susceptible host.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Affinity maturation is an intracellular process that improves antibody quality in B cells, not a population-level protection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Natural active immunity would require her own immune system to respond to infection, which her immunosuppression and lack of exposure preclude.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Passive immunity requires transferring antibodies to the individual; here she has received no antibody and is protected indirectly by community immunity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The adjuvant effect refers to boosting a vaccine's own immunogenicity, not to population-level protection of an unvaccinated person.

questions.stem: A killed, whole-pathogen (inactivated) vaccine such as the injected polio or rabies vaccine cannot infect or replicate in the host. Given this, which of the following is generally true of this vaccine type?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single dose reliably confers lifelong immunity

choices.label: B
choices.text: It generates protection mainly through cell-mediated mechanisms

choices.label: C
choices.text: It induces a strong cytotoxic (CD8+) T-cell response

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is contraindicated in immunocompromised patients

choices.label: E
choices.text: Multiple doses and boosters are required

explanation.summary: Because inactivated vaccines cannot replicate, they need multiple doses and boosters and produce mainly humoral immunity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that because there is no infection with inactivated vaccines, multiple doses are required to establish and maintain humoral immunity, and boosters are needed to sustain sufficient immunity over time. These vaccines produce mainly humoral immunity with little CD8+ T-cell response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Inactivated vaccines do not give lifelong immunity from a single dose; they specifically require repeated doses and boosters.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Inactivated vaccines work mainly through humoral (antibody) immunity, not primarily cell-mediated mechanisms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inactivated vaccines generate little CD8+ T-cell response; a robust CTL response is characteristic of live attenuated and mRNA vaccines.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Because they cannot replicate, inactivated vaccines are safe in immunocompromised patients; it is live vaccines that are contraindicated.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with a hematologic malignancy is exposed to a viral pathogen and receives an antibody product manufactured by replicating antibody molecules from a single B-cell clone. Compared with intravenous immunoglobulin, which of the following best characterizes the product he received?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds one antigen rather than many antigens

choices.label: B
choices.text: It generates memory B cells rather than transient protection

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is purified from the pooled serum of many healthy donors

choices.label: D
choices.text: It provides protection that begins only after 2-4 weeks

choices.label: E
choices.text: It transfers IgA to mucosal surfaces rather than IgG to serum

explanation.summary: Monoclonal antibodies come from a single B cell and bind a single antigen; polyclonal antibody (IVIG) comes from many B cells and binds many antigens.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists two forms of artificial passive immunity. Monoclonal antibodies are antibody molecules replicated from a single B cell that bind a single antigen. Polyclonal antibody, or intravenous immunoglobulin, consists of purified antibodies from the serum of healthy people that come from many B cells and bind many antigens. The product described, derived from one clone, is monoclonal and therefore single-antigen specific.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Both monoclonal and polyclonal products are passive immunization; neither generates memory cells, and both give only transient protection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Purification from the serum of many healthy people describes polyclonal antibody (IVIG), not a single-clone monoclonal product.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A delay of 2-4 weeks characterizes active immunization; both monoclonal and polyclonal antibody act immediately.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neither product is a mucosal IgA transfer; IgA transfer to an infant occurs naturally through breast milk.

questions.stem: A 3-week-old exclusively breastfed infant remains free of gastrointestinal infection despite household exposure to enteric pathogens. The antibody protecting the infant's gut lumen was produced by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fetal plasma cells stimulated in utero by maternal antigens

choices.label: B
choices.text: Follicular dendritic cells in the infant's Peyer patches

choices.label: C
choices.text: IgA-secreting B cells that migrated to the mother's breast

choices.label: D
choices.text: Maternal IgG transported across the placenta by FcRn

choices.label: E
choices.text: The infant's own plasma cells after a primary response

explanation.summary: Breast milk IgA is a form of natural passive immunity produced by maternal IgA-secreting B cells that have migrated to the breast.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes two examples of natural passive immunity: placental transfer of IgG via FcRn, and transfer of IgA antibodies in breast milk to a nursing infant from IgA-secreting B cells that have migrated to the breast. Protection of the gut lumen in a breastfed neonate reflects this milk-derived IgA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The antibody is made by the mother, not by fetal plasma cells; passive immunity does not involve the recipient's own cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Follicular dendritic cells present antigen to B cells; they do not secrete antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Placental transfer supplies IgG to the fetal circulation, not IgA to the gut lumen; that is the other form of natural passive immunity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A 3-week-old has not mounted a primary response to these pathogens; the protection is passively acquired, so no memory or plasma cells of the infant are involved.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with seasonal allergic rhinitis begins a treatment in which small doses of the offending allergen are administered repeatedly over many months. Which of the following changes in her immune response is the goal of this therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conversion of a Th2-dominated response to a Th1 response

choices.label: B
choices.text: Generation of cytotoxic T lymphocytes specific for the allergen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Induction of herd immunity against the allergen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neutralization of the allergen by toxoid-induced antibodies

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passive transfer of anti-allergen IgG for immediate protection

explanation.summary: Allergy therapy transfers allergen in small doses to convert the Th2 response into a Th1 response.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that vaccination is not the only setting in which antigens are transferred into a person to modulate immunity. In allergy therapy, allergens are given in small doses to convert the Th2 response to a Th1 response. Cancer immunotherapy is the other example, exposing the immune system to cancer antigens to generate a response against a non-infectious agent.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The described goal is to shift helper T-cell polarization, not to generate CTLs against an allergen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Herd immunity is population-level resistance to an infectious disease; it has no meaning for an individual's allergen response.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Toxoids are inactivated bacterial toxins used against toxin-mediated disease; allergens are not toxoids.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Allergen immunotherapy delivers antigen, not preformed antibody; it is not passive immunization.

questions.stem: In a laboratory study, a volunteer is immunized with antigen 1. Five weeks later the volunteer receives antigen 1 and antigen 2 together. Serum measured 3 weeks after the second immunization shows a large, high-affinity anti-1 response. Which of the following best describes the expected anti-2 response at the same time point?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A primary response identical in magnitude and affinity to the anti-1 response

choices.label: B
choices.text: A primary response, smaller and of lower affinity than the anti-1 response

choices.label: C
choices.text: A secondary response equal in magnitude to the anti-1 response

choices.label: D
choices.text: A secondary response, because memory cells respond to any co-administered antigen

choices.label: E
choices.text: An absent response, because antigen 1 memory cells suppress new responses

explanation.summary: Immunologic memory is antigen-specific, so a newly introduced antigen elicits only a primary response even when given alongside a recall antigen.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's Figure 2 shows that when antigen 1 is given first, memory B cells and anti-1 antibodies form. When antigen 1 and antigen 2 are later given together, the anti-1 response is greater in both quantity and quality (affinity). Because memory is antigen-specific, there is no memory to antigen 2, so the anti-2 response is a primary response: lower titer and lower affinity than the secondary anti-1 response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A primary response is smaller and lower in affinity than the secondary anti-1 response; they are not identical.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The anti-2 response is primary, not secondary, and is smaller than the boosted anti-1 response.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Memory cells are specific for antigen 1; co-administration does not let them respond to an unrelated antigen 2.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A primary anti-2 response does occur; nothing in the brick suggests memory cells to one antigen suppress responses to another.

questions.stem: Public health officials calculate that a population must reach roughly 95% immunity to halt transmission of pathogen X but only about 70% immunity to halt transmission of pathogen Y. Which of the following best accounts for the difference between these two thresholds?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The adjuvant used in each vaccine

choices.label: B
choices.text: The half-life of antibodies against each pathogen

choices.label: C
choices.text: The infectivity of each pathogen

choices.label: D
choices.text: The number of booster doses in each vaccine schedule

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whether each vaccine is live attenuated or inactivated

explanation.summary: The percentage of a population that must be immune for herd immunity ranges from 70% to 95% depending on how infectious the pathogen is.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that herd immunity results when a sufficient percentage of the population becomes immune, and that this sufficient percentage is 70-95% depending on the infectivity of the pathogen. A more infectious pathogen finds susceptible hosts more easily, so a larger fraction of the population must be immune before the pathogen can no longer travel within it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adjuvants amplify an individual's response to a vaccine and have no bearing on the population threshold.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibody half-life (roughly 3 weeks) governs how long passive immunity lasts in an individual, not the population threshold for herd immunity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Booster schedules maintain individual immunity; they do not determine what fraction of the population must be immune.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The vaccine platform affects the type of individual immune response, but the herd immunity threshold is set by the pathogen's infectivity.

questions.stem: A subunit vaccine is formulated with CpG DNA repeats to strengthen the immune response. Which of the following best describes how this added component acts at the site of vaccination?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds the antigen and delivers it directly to B cells in the lymph node follicle

choices.label: B
choices.text: It covalently links to the antigen, converting it into a T-dependent antigen for Tfh cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: It ligates pattern-recognition receptors on dendritic cells, inducing B7 and migration

choices.label: D
choices.text: It stabilizes the antigen inside a lipid nanoparticle that carries it into host cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: It supplies preformed antibody that opsonizes the antigen for uptake by phagocytes

explanation.summary: PAMP-based adjuvants such as CpG DNA and monophosphoryl lipid A are PRR ligands that activate dendritic cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that some adjuvants are pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), ligands of pattern-recognition receptors (PRRs). PAMP-based adjuvants activate dendritic cells at the site of vaccination, inducing migration to secondary lymphoid organs, MHC II presentation of available peptides, and upregulation of co-stimulatory molecules like B7. Monophosphoryl lipid A and CpG DNA repeats are the two examples given.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adjuvants act on dendritic cells and antigen presentation; they do not shuttle antigen to follicular B cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Adjuvants are explicitly not covalently bound to the vaccine antigen; covalent linkage to a protein is the strategy of conjugate vaccines.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A lipid nanoparticle stabilizes mRNA in mRNA vaccines; CpG DNA is a PRR ligand, not a delivery vehicle.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An adjuvant is not antibody; preformed antibody is passive immunization.

questions.stem: A vaccine developer compares two candidates against an intracellular viral pathogen: one is a live attenuated virus and the other is the same virus inactivated with a chemical. Only the live attenuated candidate elicits virus-specific CD8+ T cells. Which of the following best explains this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chemical inactivation destroys the antigenic structure required for any adaptive immune response

choices.label: B
choices.text: The attenuated virus carries alum, which enhances antigen uptake and presentation by dendritic cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: The attenuated virus causes a self-limited infection, so infected cells present viral peptides on MHC class I

choices.label: D
choices.text: The attenuated virus is covalently linked to a carrier protein that recruits follicular helper T cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: The inactivated virus acts as a T-independent antigen that stimulates B cells without T-cell involvement

explanation.summary: Live attenuated vaccines generate CTLs because the self-limited infection lets infected host cells present peptides on MHC class I.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that LAVs are most effective against intracellular pathogens because a self-limiting infection allows infected cells to present peptides on MHC I and stimulate a CTL response. The infection is also pro-inflammatory, recruiting phagocytes and lymphocytes to the site. Inactivated vaccines cannot infect cells, so little CD8+ T-cell immunity is ever established with them.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Inactivated vaccines retain the diversity and structure of the antigens needed to elicit an immune response; they simply generate mainly humoral and CD4+ immunity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Alum is an adjuvant added to subunit vaccines; a live attenuated virus induces immunity through infection, not through alum.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Conjugation to a carrier protein is the mechanism of conjugate polysaccharide vaccines, not of live attenuated vaccines.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inactivated whole virus contains protein and drives CD4+ T-cell and humoral immunity; it is not a T-independent antigen.

questions.stem: A healthy 25-year-old man receives an intranasal influenza vaccine at a pharmacy. Compared with the standard injected influenza vaccine, the preparation he received is best characterized as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A killed whole virus that cannot replicate in the vaccinated host

choices.label: B
choices.text: A lipid nanoparticle containing viral mRNA encoding a surface protein

choices.label: C
choices.text: A live attenuated virus that can cause a self-limited infection

choices.label: D
choices.text: A purified viral protein subunit combined with an alum adjuvant

choices.label: E
choices.text: A viral polysaccharide conjugated to a diphtheria toxoid carrier

explanation.summary: Intranasal influenza vaccine is live attenuated, whereas the standard injected influenza vaccine is inactivated.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists intranasal influenza among the live attenuated vaccines, alongside yellow fever, the Sabin oral polio vaccine, and BCG. In contrast, the standard (injected) influenza vaccine is listed among the inactivated vaccines on the US schedule. A live attenuated virus can induce a self-limited infection in an immunocompetent person.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A killed whole virus describes the injected influenza vaccine, not the intranasal preparation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: mRNA vaccines in the brick are those against SARS-CoV-2 and RSV, not the intranasal influenza vaccine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The intranasal influenza vaccine is not a subunit vaccine; it contains weakened live virus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Conjugate vaccines target encapsulated bacteria such as S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae type b, and N. meningitidis, not influenza virus.

questions.stem: In a region that relies on the oral polio vaccine, surveillance identifies several cases of paralytic polio in immunocompetent children caused by a strain genetically derived from the vaccine itself rather than by wild-type virus. Which of the following changes in vaccination policy most directly addresses this problem?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adding alum to the oral polio vaccine to strengthen the response

choices.label: B
choices.text: Administering polyclonal antibody with each oral dose

choices.label: C
choices.text: Conjugating the oral polio vaccine to a carrier protein

choices.label: D
choices.text: Restricting the oral polio vaccine to immunocompromised children

choices.label: E
choices.text: Switching to the injected (Salk) polio vaccine, which is killed

explanation.summary: Vaccine-derived polio arises from reversion of the live attenuated Sabin vaccine; many countries therefore give only the killed Salk vaccine.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that the polio LAV occasionally reverts, causing infection in immunocompetent people, and that at this time there are more cases of vaccine-derived polio than naturally circulating polio. To combat this, many countries only give the Salk (injected) polio vaccine, which is killed and therefore cannot revert to a virulent form.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alum amplifies the immune response; it does nothing to prevent the attenuated virus from reverting.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Passive antibody gives short-lived protection and does not eliminate the replicating, potentially reverting vaccine virus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Conjugation converts a polysaccharide into a T-dependent antigen; it is irrelevant to a live viral vaccine's reversion risk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Live attenuated vaccines are contraindicated in immunocompromised people, in whom they can cause severe or fatal infection.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman traveling abroad receives the hepatitis A vaccine. Which of the following best describes the contents of this vaccine?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Attenuated hepatitis A virus that can enter cells but not replicate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hepatitis A capsid proteins assembled into a virus-like particle

choices.label: C
choices.text: Messenger RNA encoding a hepatitis A protein in a lipid nanoparticle

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recombinant hepatitis A surface protein produced in yeast cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whole hepatitis A virus inactivated by heat, radiation, or chemicals

explanation.summary: Hepatitis A vaccine is an inactivated (killed) whole-pathogen vaccine.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists hepatitis A among the inactivated vaccines on the US schedule, with the injected influenza vaccine and the injected (Salk) polio vaccine; anthrax and rabies are other killed vaccines. Inactivated vaccines are produced by inactivating a whole pathogen, often through heat, radiation, or chemicals, leaving it unable to infect or replicate while retaining its antigenic structure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An attenuated virus that enters cells describes a live attenuated vaccine; hepatitis A vaccine is killed.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A virus-like particle vaccine describes the HPV vaccine, not hepatitis A.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The mRNA vaccines described are against SARS-CoV-2 and RSV, not hepatitis A.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Recombinant surface antigen made in yeast describes the hepatitis B vaccine, not hepatitis A.

questions.stem: The pertussis component of the DTaP vaccine given to infants today differs from the pertussis vaccine introduced in the 1940s. Which of the following best describes the current pertussis component and the reason it replaced the original?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a capsular polysaccharide conjugated to tetanus toxoid, chosen to improve infant responses

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a live attenuated bacterium, chosen because a single dose provides full protection

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a whole-cell inactivated bacterium, chosen because it induces cytotoxic T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is acellular, containing 1-5 purified antigens, and is less reactogenic than the whole-cell vaccine

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is an mRNA construct, chosen because it can be manufactured at lower cost

explanation.summary: The original whole-cell inactivated pertussis vaccine was replaced by a less reactogenic acellular vaccine of 1-5 purified antigens.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that the pertussis vaccine introduced in the 1940s was an inactivated whole-cell vaccine that cut US pertussis cases from roughly 200,000 per year to roughly 1,000. The current pertussis vaccine is acellular, containing 1-5 purified antigens, and is less reactogenic than the whole-cell vaccine. Pertussis is therefore listed among the protein-based (subunit) vaccines on the US schedule.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Conjugate vaccines target encapsulated bacteria such as S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae type b, and N. meningitidis, not pertussis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: No live attenuated pertussis vaccine is described; the current vaccine is acellular and, like other subunit vaccines, requires boosters.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The whole-cell inactivated vaccine was the original 1940s product that was replaced; inactivated vaccines generate mainly humoral immunity, not CTLs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The mRNA vaccines named are against SARS-CoV-2 and RSV; pertussis vaccine is protein-based.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman asks whether the mRNA vaccine she is about to receive contains an aluminum adjuvant. Her physician explains that it does not, but that another component of the formulation performs the adjuvant function. Which of the following is that component?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A harmless adenovirus that carries the mRNA into cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: A tetanus toxoid carrier protein covalently linked to the mRNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monophosphoryl lipid A bound to the spike protein

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pooled polyclonal immunoglobulin mixed with the mRNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: The lipid nanoparticle that also delivers the mRNA into cells

explanation.summary: In mRNA vaccines the lipid nanoparticle both stabilizes and delivers the mRNA and acts as an adjuvant.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the mRNA is stabilized using a lipid nanoparticle, which allows the mRNA to enter cells and acts as an adjuvant. Once inside host cells, the mRNA directs production of viral proteins that are presented on class I and II MHC molecules. No separate aluminum salt is needed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A harmless carrier virus is the basis of viral vector vaccines, not mRNA vaccines.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Toxoid carrier proteins are used in conjugate polysaccharide vaccines; adjuvants are not covalently bound to the vaccine antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Monophosphoryl lipid A is a PAMP-based adjuvant example, but the brick identifies the lipid nanoparticle as the adjuvant in mRNA vaccines; and adjuvants are not bound to the antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Polyclonal immunoglobulin is passive immunization and is not a vaccine component.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old nursing student receives the hepatitis B vaccine before beginning clinical rotations. Which of the following best describes the antigen in this vaccine?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An adenovirus vector carrying the hepatitis B surface antigen gene

choices.label: B
choices.text: Attenuated hepatitis B virus that establishes a self-limited infection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hepatitis B surface antigen conjugated to diphtheria toxoid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hepatitis B surface antigen made in yeast cells from the viral genetic code

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whole hepatitis B virus inactivated with chemicals

explanation.summary: Hepatitis B vaccine is a recombinant subunit vaccine: viral surface antigen produced in yeast from the pathogen's genetic code.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes a recombinant vaccine as one manufactured using the genetic code from the pathogen and a producer cell. The hepatitis B vaccine is made of recombinant hepatitis B surface antigen (viral) made in yeast cells. It is a protein-based subunit vaccine on the US schedule.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Viral vector technology is described for Ebola and one COVID-19 vaccine, not for hepatitis B.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hepatitis B vaccine contains no live virus; it is a purified recombinant protein.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Conjugation to a toxoid is used for bacterial capsular polysaccharides, not for a viral protein antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chemically inactivated whole virus describes killed vaccines such as hepatitis A, injected polio, and rabies, not hepatitis B.

questions.stem: The parent of a 12-year-old girl scheduled to receive the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine is worried that the vaccine could give her daughter an HPV infection. Which of the following features of the vaccine best addresses this concern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It consists of a viral polysaccharide that cannot be taken up by host cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: It consists of an attenuated virus that can enter cells but cannot replicate

choices.label: C
choices.text: It consists of mRNA that is degraded before any viral protein is produced

choices.label: D
choices.text: It consists of viral capsid proteins assembled into a particle that lacks the viral genome

choices.label: E
choices.text: It consists of whole virus inactivated by heat so that it cannot enter cells

explanation.summary: HPV vaccine is a virus-like particle vaccine: capsid proteins without any viral genome, so it cannot cause infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes a virus-like particle vaccine as one that contains the proteins that make up the capsid (outer shell) of the virion but does not contain the genome; the HPV vaccine is composed of a virus-like particle. With no genetic material, the particle cannot replicate or establish infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HPV vaccine antigen is capsid protein, not polysaccharide; polysaccharide vaccines are made from bacterial capsules.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An attenuated virus that enters cells describes a live attenuated vaccine, which HPV vaccine is not.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HPV vaccine contains no mRNA; and mRNA vaccines do produce viral protein in host cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HPV vaccine is not a killed whole-virus vaccine; it is a protein-based subunit vaccine.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman at 34 weeks' gestation receives the recombinant respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccine. Her newborn is protected against severe RSV infection after birth. This protection is expected to last approximately how long?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1 year

choices.label: B
choices.text: 3 weeks

choices.label: C
choices.text: 3-6 months

choices.label: D
choices.text: 3-6 weeks

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lifelong, because memory B cells are transferred

explanation.summary: Maternal RSV vaccination protects the neonate through transplacental IgG, which wanes at 3-6 months after birth.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the recombinant RSV vaccine is recommended during pregnancy because infants are at particular risk of severe infection. Vaccination of the pregnant individual induces IgG generation, which crosses the placenta, so neonates born to a vaccinated parent are protected from RSV until the transplacental antibodies wane at 3-6 months following birth.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Transplacental antibody has waned well before 1 year; protection ends at 3-6 months.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Roughly 3 weeks is the half-life of antibody molecules, but the brick states that transplacental protection persists until 3-6 months.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick gives the window in months, not weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Only IgG crosses the placenta; memory cells are not transferred, so the infant's protection is passive and temporary.

questions.stem: A 15-month-old boy is inadvertently given a plain (unconjugated) pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine instead of the conjugate vaccine. Which of the following best describes the expected immune response to this dose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A cytotoxic T-cell response, because the polysaccharide is presented on MHC class I

choices.label: B
choices.text: A primary response now that is boosted to a strong secondary response by a second polysaccharide dose

choices.label: C
choices.text: High-affinity antibodies generated through affinity maturation driven by follicular helper T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Long-lived IgG1 and IgG3 antibody production with induction of polysaccharide-specific memory B cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: No meaningful antibody response, because infants under 2 years do not respond to polysaccharide antigens

explanation.summary: Plain polysaccharide vaccines are T-independent and produce no immune response in infants younger than 2 years.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's Figure 7 lists the features of a polysaccharide vaccine: no production of memory B cells, short-lived antibody production, no affinity maturation, and no immune response in infants under 2 years. Because polysaccharides are T-independent antigens that do not allow T cells to help B cells, a 15-month-old cannot mount a useful response; the conjugate vaccine exists precisely to improve responses in infants.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Polysaccharides are not presented on MHC class I and do not generate CTLs; subunit vaccines produce only humoral immunity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Polysaccharide vaccines do not generate memory, so a repeat dose does not produce a secondary response; and an infant under 2 years does not respond at all.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Affinity maturation requires T-cell help; polysaccharide vaccines produce low-affinity antibody with no affinity maturation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Long-lived IgG1/IgG3 production and memory B-cell induction are features of the protein-polysaccharide conjugate vaccine, not the plain polysaccharide.

questions.stem: A conjugate vaccine composed of Haemophilus influenzae type b capsular polysaccharide linked to tetanus toxoid is given to a child. In the lymph node, a polysaccharide-specific B cell binds the vaccine and internalizes the entire complex. Which of the following is then displayed on this B cell's MHC class II molecules to obtain help from follicular helper T cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fragments of the capsular polysaccharide

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lipid A from the vaccine adjuvant

choices.label: C
choices.text: Peptides derived from the B-cell receptor itself

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peptides derived from the tetanus toxoid carrier

choices.label: E
choices.text: The intact vaccine complex bound to the B-cell receptor

explanation.summary: In a conjugate vaccine, the polysaccharide-specific B cell presents carrier-protein peptides on MHC class II to gain Tfh help.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the mechanism: follicular dendritic cells present the polysaccharide fragment to B cells, which recognize and bind the polysaccharide component and then internalize the entire complex. The B cells process the complex and present protein peptides on their own MHC class II molecules to T follicular helper (Tfh) cells, gaining CD40L and cytokine signals. This is how the polysaccharide is converted into a T-dependent antigen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: MHC class II presents peptides, not polysaccharide fragments; this is exactly why a plain polysaccharide cannot recruit T-cell help.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Adjuvants are not covalently bound to the antigen and are not what is presented on MHC II to Tfh cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The B cell presents peptides from the internalized carrier protein, not from its own receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The B-cell receptor binds the polysaccharide on the surface, but the complex is internalized and processed; intact complexes are not displayed on MHC II.

questions.stem: Conjugate vaccines used in the United States link the bacterial polysaccharide to either tetanus or diphtheria toxoid. In an infant who has previously received the first doses of DTaP, which of the following is the immunologic advantage of choosing these particular carrier proteins?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Memory T cells specific for the toxoid already exist and are activated by dendritic cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: The toxoid acts as a PAMP that ligates pattern-recognition receptors on dendritic cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: The toxoid allows the polysaccharide to be presented on MHC class I to CD8+ cytotoxic T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: The toxoid blocks affinity maturation, preventing autoreactive antibodies from forming

choices.label: E
choices.text: The toxoid neutralizes bacterial toxin released at the injection site by the vaccine

explanation.summary: Using tetanus or diphtheria toxoid as the carrier exploits memory T cells already generated by prior DTaP vaccination.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that conjugate vaccines take advantage of the memory T-cell response to specific peptides to generate a long-lived, high-affinity humoral response to the polysaccharide. Those used in the USA are conjugated to either the tetanus or diphtheria toxoid; dendritic cells at the site of vaccination migrate to the lymph node and present toxoid to memory T cells (generated from past DTaP or other vaccines) to activate them, which then provide help to polysaccharide-specific B cells.

whyWrongByChoice.B: PAMP-based adjuvants (monophosphoryl lipid A, CpG DNA) ligate PRRs; a toxoid carrier is a protein antigen recognized by T cells, and adjuvants are not covalently bound to antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Conjugation converts the polysaccharide into a T-dependent antigen presented on MHC class II, not class I.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Conjugation promotes, rather than blocks, affinity maturation; that is the purpose of recruiting T-cell help.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A toxoid is an inactivated toxin used as an antigen; it does not itself neutralize toxin, and no toxin is released at the injection site.

questions.stem: A plain (unconjugated) meningococcal polysaccharide vaccine produces a high-affinity, neutralizing antibody response in a 19-year-old but a poor response in a 2-year-old. Which of the following best explains the adolescent's robust response to this T-independent antigen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adolescents have a larger thymus that supplies more helper T cells to the germinal center

choices.label: B
choices.text: Adolescents have more dendritic cells that can present polysaccharide on MHC class II

choices.label: C
choices.text: Polysaccharides become T-dependent antigens once the immune system matures after puberty

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prior natural exposure or conjugate vaccination has already generated memory B cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transplacental maternal IgG persists in adolescents and neutralizes the polysaccharide

explanation.summary: Adolescents and adults respond to plain polysaccharide vaccines because prior exposure has already produced high-affinity memory B cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that young children (roughly five and under) do not respond well to polysaccharide vaccines against S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae type b, and N. meningitidis, but adolescents and adults do. These pathogens circulate, and by adolescence most people have been exposed, by conjugate vaccination or naturally. They have developed excellent memory B cells capable of generating a neutralizing, high-affinity response even to the T-independent polysaccharide antigen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The polysaccharide remains T-independent; T-cell help is not the source of the adolescent's response, and the brick does not attribute it to thymic size.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The difference is explained by pre-existing memory B cells, not by dendritic cell numbers or adjuvant responsiveness.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Polysaccharides are T-independent antigens at any age; they become T-dependent only when conjugated to a protein.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transplacental maternal IgG wanes within months of birth and is not present in a 19-year-old.

questions.stem: A vaccine against Ebola virus, introduced in 2019, is manufactured by inserting a portion of the Ebola genome into the genome of a harmless virus. After injection, which of the following best describes how the Ebola antigen is generated in the recipient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Attenuated Ebola virus enters host cells and establishes a self-limited infection that presents viral peptides

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ebola mRNA stabilized in a lipid nanoparticle enters host cells and is translated by host ribosomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inactivated whole Ebola virions are taken up by dendritic cells and processed for MHC class II presentation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Purified recombinant Ebola glycoprotein is taken up and processed directly by antigen-presenting cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: The carrier virus replicates in host cells, and its genome, including the Ebola segment, is transcribed and translated

explanation.summary: Viral vector vaccines use a replicating harmless host virus to express a pathogen gene inside the recipient's cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes viral vector vaccines as manufactured by introducing a portion of the genome of the pathogenic virus into the genome of a harmless host virus. The host virus replicates in the vaccinated individual without causing disease, and the full genome, including the portion from the pathogen, is transcribed and translated so the antigen can be presented in MHC. This technology was introduced in 2019 for Ebola and used in one of the initial COVID-19 vaccines with adenovirus as the vector.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A live attenuated vaccine uses the weakened pathogen itself; a viral vector vaccine uses a different, harmless virus carrying only a piece of the pathogen's genome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An mRNA vaccine delivers mRNA in a lipid nanoparticle without any virus; the vector vaccine delivers DNA in a carrier virus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inactivated whole virions describe killed vaccines, which contain no replicating virus and generate mainly humoral immunity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Purified protein describes a recombinant subunit vaccine; in a vector vaccine the antigen is synthesized inside host cells.

questions.stem: A vaccine is being designed against a virus for which protection requires both neutralizing antibodies and virus-specific cytotoxic T lymphocytes. Which of the following vaccine types would be expected to generate both cell-mediated and humoral immunity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conjugate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inactivated

choices.label: C
choices.text: Polysaccharide

choices.label: D
choices.text: Toxoid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Viral vector

explanation.summary: Live attenuated, mRNA, and viral vector vaccines generate cell-mediated and humoral immunity; inactivated and subunit vaccines are mainly humoral.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's Table 1 assigns 'cell-mediated and humoral' responses to live attenuated, mRNA, and viral vector vaccines, and 'mainly humoral' responses to inactivated and subunit vaccines (recombinant, polysaccharide, conjugate, toxoid). The summary adds that LAVs, mRNA, and viral vector vaccines generate a full immune response and are effective against intracellular pathogens. Viral vector vaccines stimulate strong cell-mediated and humoral responses because the antigen is made inside host cells and presented in MHC.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Conjugate vaccines improve the humoral response to polysaccharide by recruiting T-cell help, but they remain subunit vaccines with a mainly humoral response.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Inactivated vaccines produce mainly humoral immunity with little CD8+ T-cell immunity ever established.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Polysaccharide vaccines are subunit vaccines producing only humoral immunity, and low-affinity antibody without memory at that.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Toxoid is a subunit vaccine and generates mainly humoral immunity (antibodies that neutralize toxin).

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl developed anaphylaxis within minutes of receiving the first dose of a vaccine. She is now due for the second dose of the same vaccine. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Administer the full dose after pretreatment with an antihistamine and observe for 30 minutes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Administer the second dose at half the usual volume under observation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Defer the dose until age 5 years, when allergic reactions become less likely

choices.label: D
choices.text: Do not give this vaccine again; a prior severe allergic reaction to a component contraindicates it

choices.label: E
choices.text: Switch to a live attenuated formulation of the same vaccine, which is less allergenic

explanation.summary: A severe allergic reaction such as anaphylaxis to a vaccine component is a contraindication to further administration of that vaccine.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists the circumstances in which vaccines should not be administered: severe allergic reaction (e.g., anaphylaxis) to a component of the vaccine, known severe immunodeficiency for the patient or close contacts (live attenuated vaccines), and pregnancy (most LAVs). Unlike the immunodeficiency and pregnancy contraindications, which apply only to LAVs, prior anaphylaxis applies to any vaccine type.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pretreatment does not remove the contraindication; the brick does not describe any premedication strategy for a previously anaphylactic patient.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A reduced dose is not described as a way around this contraindication; anaphylaxis to a component means the vaccine should not be administered.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Deferral is the approach for a severe acute illness, not for a prior anaphylactic reaction, which is a contraindication rather than a timing issue.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Live attenuated status is irrelevant to component allergy, and there is no basis for calling an LAV less allergenic.

questions.stem: A 15-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department with a temperature of 39.8 C (103.6 F), lethargy, and poor oral intake. His record shows he is due for his MMR and varicella vaccines. Which of the following is the most appropriate action regarding vaccination today?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Administer both vaccines now so that no scheduled doses are missed

choices.label: B
choices.text: Administer both vaccines together with an antipyretic

choices.label: C
choices.text: Administer only the varicella vaccine today and delay MMR

choices.label: D
choices.text: Defer both vaccines until the acute illness has resolved

choices.label: E
choices.text: Replace both vaccines with a dose of intravenous immunoglobulin

explanation.summary: Vaccination is deferred during a severe acute illness so the current illness can be diagnosed without confounding by vaccine adverse effects.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that vaccination should be deferred if the patient is grappling with a severe acute illness, allowing the physician to accurately diagnose the current illness without being confounded by potential adverse effects from vaccine administration. The summary lists 'is acutely ill' among the situations in which vaccination is contraindicated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Giving vaccines during a severe acute febrile illness would confound the evaluation of the illness; deferral, not adherence to schedule, is recommended.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An antipyretic does not remove the reason for deferral, which is diagnostic clarity rather than fever control.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both are live vaccines and both should be deferred; there is no basis for giving one and not the other during acute illness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IVIG is passive immunization for antibody-deficient or exposed patients; it is not a substitute for routine active immunization.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman who is 16 weeks pregnant brings her 4-year-old son for his second dose of the varicella vaccine. She asks whether the live vaccine should be postponed because of her pregnancy. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Give the dose only after serology confirms the mother is immune, since contacts of nonimmune people cannot receive it

choices.label: B
choices.text: Give the dose today; a pregnant household contact is not a contraindication, though she should avoid any vaccine rash

choices.label: C
choices.text: Give the son varicella immunoglobulin instead of the vaccine until after the delivery

choices.label: D
choices.text: Postpone the dose until after delivery, because live vaccines are contraindicated for close contacts of pregnant people

choices.label: E
choices.text: Postpone the dose until after delivery, because the attenuated virus could revert to its virulent form in the child

explanation.summary: Pregnancy is a contraindication for the pregnant person receiving an LAV, but not for vaccinating her close contacts.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's case connection confirms that pregnancy is a contraindication to the mother receiving the varicella vaccine, but there is no contraindication to giving the vaccine to close contacts. In rare cases the self-limiting infection from the live varicella vaccine can cause a blister-like rash, and she should avoid contact with the rash because it may contain replicating virus. By contrast, known severe immunodeficiency is a contraindication for LAVs in both the patient and their close contacts.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick does not condition the son's vaccination on maternal serology; his vaccination is not contraindicated regardless.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immunoglobulin is passive immunization that provides only short-lived protection without memory; it is not a substitute for the child's scheduled active immunization.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The close-contact restriction for live vaccines applies to contacts of people with known severe immunodeficiency, not to contacts of pregnant people.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reversion is a rare risk of unstable attenuation and is discussed for the oral polio vaccine; it is not the basis for any contraindication in a healthy child.
